Verdict

Outcome
partial
Evidence

[F1] the two golds rank the tokenizers alike, with τ above its bar; [F2] the manually checked forms rank them differently from all forms, with τ below its bar; [F3] only Unigram's morpheme-boundary F1 still rises at the largest vocabulary, while compression improves everywhere.

Discussion
  • The Sloleks 3.2 split ranks the tokenizers as the corrected heuristic does, but which forms are scored matters more than which gold cuts them. The two golds put the same algorithms in the same order and only swap vocabulary sizes within an algorithm ([F1]). Scoring the manually checked forms alone reorders the tokenizers ([F2]), so the first bar holds and the second fails: the automatic-rows reading the Verdict rule named.
  • The reordering is a word-class effect the design did not anticipate. The manual slice holds about half the share of nouns that all forms hold, and the word classes rank the tokenizers apart ([F4]). A pooled morph score therefore follows the class mix of the scored set, and is only comparable between sets with the same mix.
  • The verdict rule named this split without an outcome word, and the levelling rule reads noise as movement. The split takes the word partial, added to the rule at conclusion: yes for the gold, no for the slice. Q1's quarter rule turns morpheme-boundary F1 changes narrower than their intervals into falls or gains ([F3]). A follow-up inherits the Sloleks gold, the manual-first score and a band rule for levelling.
Adoption candidate

The project's shared tokenizer sweep, scripts/sweep_tokenizers.py, scores on the Sloleks 3.2 gold with the manual-forms score first. The pieces to lift are the Sloleks gold builder and the lexeme holdout in slm4ie/tokenizers/morphology.py, and the Slovene word-class fix in the heuristic gold. The capped alphabet and the Unigram document cut in slm4ie/tokenizers/train.py and the lexeme bootstrap of analysis.py go with them.

Next
  • The next experiment, on new morph metrics, reports every morph score on the manual forms first and per word class beside the pooled score. It reads levelling with a band from the bootstrap intervals rather than the quarter rule ([Q1]).
  • A retrain of MorphBPE and MorphPiece with a morpheme table built from the Sloleks split, as its own experiment. MorphBPE at 128k trains for more than a day on one core.
  • An audit of the automatic noun rows of Sloleks 3.2, the class where the manual and the all-forms rankings agree least ([F4]).
  • A curation fix for the NUL characters, byte zero, left in the corpus where a letter was lost upstream; delivery work.
Limitations
  • Both golds cover inflection only; derivation and compounding are unscored, so a tokenizer that cuts prefixes well gets no credit.
  • Rank agreement is over 24 tokenizers, so τ moves in steps of about 0.007 and its point estimate can sit at the edge of its bootstrap interval.
  • The morpheme table of MorphBPE and MorphPiece comes from the corrected heuristic, so their scores under the Sloleks gold may understate what a table from the Sloleks split would give.
  • Morpheme-boundary F1 is pooled over forms with one count each; the frequency-weighted score was read beside the clauses only.

Question

Statement

The tokenizers rank the same on morpheme-boundary F1 whether the gold is the project's lemma-alignment heuristic, with its word-class tags corrected, or the stem-ending split that the Sloleks 3.2 authors released. Scoring on the manually checked forms alone gives the same ranking as scoring on all forms.

Rationale
  • The morph metrics so far rest on a heuristic gold. The heuristic aligns each inflected form to its lemma (dictionary form) and cuts where they first differ, with rules for the usual stem changes. The June sweep notes call it silver gold and read its scores only as relative comparators between tokenizers.
  • That heuristic never split a noun. It keeps a form whole when the form's morphosyntactic tag starts with a letter it takes for an invariant word class. Those letters follow the English tag set, where S is a preposition, but Sloleks uses the Slovene tag set, where S is a noun. The June scores therefore measured mostly verbs and adjectives, and the morpheme table that MorphBPE and MorphPiece train on held no noun splits.
  • Sloleks 3.2 gives a split from the lexicon's own authors. Each inflected form is cut into the stem shared by its whole paradigm and the ending, from the inflection patterns of the lexicon. About 30% of the forms are manually checked, and the rest are generated automatically. It covers inflection only, not derivation or compounding.
  • The two golds cut differently even where the heuristic does cut. The heuristic stops at the first difference from the lemma, so a fleeting vowel or an augment moves the cut: the heuristic gives binokularn·a, Sloleks 3.2 gives binokular·na. If such cuts reorder the tokenizers, the June morph conclusions do not hold.
  • The data can carry the bars, by the counts on disk. Sloleks 3.2 holds 2.89 million distinct forms in nouns, adjectives, verbs and adverbs, 0.86 million of them on manually checked lexemes. Of the 2.80 million forms both golds cover, the uncorrected heuristic agrees on the cut in 23%, mostly verbs and adjectives, and leaves 91% of nouns unsplit. Holding out a fifth of the lexemes leaves about half a million scored forms. Counts in forms per word class and checking status.
Predictions
Every clause is read on the 24 tokenizers (six algorithms at 16k, 32k, 64k and 128k vocabulary), trained on the training side of the corpus split ([D2], [D3]). Each is scored on the same held-out forms under each gold, from lexemes no morpheme table saw ([D1], [D4]). Rank agreement is Kendall's τ over the 24 tokenizers on morpheme-boundary F1, with a 95% bootstrap interval over lexemes ([D6]). Shown as the clause table at the top of the page.
  • Verdict rule: confirmed when H1 and H2 both hold; refuted when H1 is refuted; inconclusive when an interval of τ straddles its bar. H2 refuted with H1 confirmed is the automatic-rows reading: the golds agree, but the score is reported on manual forms first. Q1 is read beside that outcome and does not change it. — Note added 2026-10-25 at conclusion: the automatic-rows reading takes the outcome word partial, since the rule named the reading without a word and a split of the bars takes neither side's word.
  • Read beside the clauses, not as clauses: forms scored per gold and slice; τ for H1 and H2 on the 16 tokenizers that train without a morpheme table ([D5]); morpheme-boundary F1 on multi-token forms only ([D7]), without forms that have no ending ([D8]) and weighted by corpus frequency ([D9]); τ against the MorphScore v2 Slovene ranking ([D10]); the share of each vocabulary that occurs rarely in the training and evaluation samples ([D12]); the uncorrected June heuristic's scores, as the size of the tag bug; training time and peak memory of the 128k tokenizers.

Setup

Inputs

The shared curated corpus, the Sloleks 3.1 lexicon as the heuristic's source, the Sloleks 3.2 stem-ending split, the Sloleks word relations and the MorphScore v2 Slovene set, described in ## Datasets.

Method / factors

One pass from a corpus split and two golds to two rank agreements.

  • Split the corpus 80/20 by document within each source, and draw a training sample and an evaluation sample from the two sides ([D3], [M1], [M2]).
  • Build the Sloleks 3.2 gold, one form per row, and mark each form manual or automatic ([D1], [M3]).
  • Build the heuristic gold from Sloleks 3.1 with the Slovene word-class tags ([M4]).
  • Split the lexemes 80/20, build the morpheme table from the training side, and keep the held-out forms for scoring ([D4], [M5]).
  • Train the six algorithms at four vocabulary sizes on the training sample, the character-level ones on a capped alphabet ([D2], [D14], [M6]).
  • Score all 24 tokenizers on the held-out forms under each gold and slice, and on the evaluation sample for the corpus metrics ([M7]).
  • Rank the tokenizers per gold and slice, and compute τ with its interval for H1 and H2 ([M8]).
  • Factors: the gold (corrected heuristic, Sloleks 3.2) and the slice (manual, all) are scientific. The algorithm and the vocabulary size span the population being ranked. The training sample and the morpheme table are fixed ([D2]).
Metrics

Primary Kendall's τ between tokenizer rankings on morpheme-boundary F1; secondary Morph-Edit-Distance, Morph-Consistency, fertility, compression and Rényi efficiency — each defined in experiments/GLOSSARY.md.

Protocol

Training each of the 24 tokenizers is one tracked run. Scoring is deterministic and recomputed by analysis.py from the tokenizer files, the golds and the evaluation sample, with no further runs.

Datasets

Sloleks stem-ending split

One item is one lexeme of the Sloleks authors' release DSBS__inflect_morph_seg__2026-07.tsv, with its manual or automatic status and each inflected form cut into the paradigm stem and the ending. The authors shared it from the CJVT Nextcloud in July 2026; it is cited as Sloleks 3.1. It is converted to the shared tokenization/sloleks_inflection.jsonl.gz and cut into the Sloleks gold by [D1].

Sloleks 3.1 lexicon

One item is one lemma of Sloleks 3.1 (CLARIN.SI 11356/2080) with its inflected forms and tags, converted to the shared tokenization/sloleks.jsonl.gz in June 2026. The corrected heuristic gold is aligned from it; its rows sit in the same table as the Sloleks gold's.

June gold

The heuristic gold the June sweep saved before the tag fix (tokenizers/morph_lexicon_infl.jsonl.gz), read beside the clauses only. The shared sweep registry now builds the corrected gold, so this file is the only copy of the June one. Its rows sit in the same table.

Scored-form golds

The Sloleks, heuristic and June golds cut to the held-out forms all three cover ([D4]), frozen as final/morph-golds-heldout-forms/ under the experiment's data folder; every tokenizer is scored on these forms. Each form carries the held-out lexeme it is resampled under ([D6]); the lexeme counts sit in the gold table.

Held-out form counts

One item is one scored form with its count in the evaluation sample ([D9]), frozen as final/heldout-form-counts/. A form holding a digit or hyphen (a380, APZ-ja) never matches a run of letters, so it keeps only the weight of one that every form gets before its count is added ([D9]). The forms seen, the forms that can never be counted and the occurrences per word class sit in the gold table.

Curated corpus split

One item is one document of the shared corpus after sentence dedup (pretrain/06_sentence_dedup, 18 sources, built 2026-10-08). Each source's documents are split 80/20 into a training and an evaluation side ([D3]), and a sample is drawn from each side. A word here is a whitespace-separated token, so the totals exceed the statistics stage's word counts.

Lexeme split

The Sloleks 3.2 lexemes split 80/20 within each word class and checking status ([D4]); the morpheme table is built from the training side and the clauses are scored on the held-out forms.

Sloleks word relations

One item is one derived lemma of the Sloleks 2.0 word relations (CLARIN.SI 11356/1986) cut into morphemes, converted to the shared tokenization/sloleks_relations.jsonl.gz; it joins the morpheme table only.

MorphScore v2 Slovene set

One item is one word form from the Slovene UD treebank SSJ, cut into stem and affixes by its longest substring shared with the lemma (Arnett, Hudspeth & O'Connor 2025, arXiv:2507.06378). It is downloaded from the authors' Hugging Face dataset at the revision of 2025-07-10 (CC BY-SA 4.0) and converted to the shared tokenization/morphscore_slovenian.jsonl.gz. MorphScore v2's default filters keep the first occurrence of each item, with its stem equal to its lemma and no digit in the form. The result is frozen as final/morphscore-slovene-items/ and scores the 16 tokenizers without a morpheme table as an outside gold ([D10]).

Methods

M1Split every source's documents 80/20 into a training side and an evaluation sideslm4ie/tokenizers/corpus.py::fit_corpus_split

Input

The shared curated corpus pretrain/06_sentence_dedup/, one JSONL record per document with its id and text, in one folder per source (18 sources).

Output

corpus_split.json in the experiment's final/sweep-vocab-size/: one rank threshold per source, the documents, words and bytes on each side, and a fingerprint of the corpus shard set. It is the input of [M2].

How
  1. Each document gets a rank: the first eight bytes of the BLAKE2b hash of <source>/<id>, read as an integer.
  2. Within each source the documents are sorted by rank, and the first ntrain=round(N·s) form the training side, where N is the source's document count and s is corpus.split.train_share. The rank of the next document is the source's threshold, so a document's side follows from its rank alone.
  3. The fingerprint is a SHA-256 hash over every shard's path, size and modification time. A later step that reads the corpus refuses the split when the fingerprint differs, since the corpus changed under it. Training reads only the sample, so it does not check.
  4. The split is by id, so two documents with the same text but different ids can sit on different sides ([D3]).
Code
slm4ie/tokenizers/corpus.py::fit_corpus_split
Settings
corpus.root (the corpus folder), corpus.split.train_share (share of each source on the training side), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml

M2Draw a training sample and an evaluation sample in proportion to each side's sourcesslm4ie/tokenizers/corpus.py::materialize_sample

Input

The corpus and the split of [M1].

Output

corpus_sample.txt.gz (training) and eval_sample.txt.gz (evaluation), one document text per line, each with a .sources.json sidecar giving the side and the documents, words and bytes drawn per source. The training sample feeds the tokenizer training of [M6]; the evaluation sample feeds the corpus metrics.

How
  1. Each source's quota is the byte budget times the source's share of that side's bytes.
  2. Each source's shards are read in an order shuffled by the side's seed, and only documents on the side are taken, until the quota is met.
  3. A sample reused later is refused if its sidecar names the other side. Training and scoring never redraw a sample, even when forced; only the sample --force step does.
Code
slm4ie/tokenizers/corpus.py::materialize_sample
Settings
corpus.budget.max_bytes (training budget, 2 GB), corpus.budget.seed (training shuffle seed), eval.corpus_budget.max_bytes (evaluation budget, 200 MB), eval.corpus_budget.seed (evaluation shuffle seed), corpus.budget.source_weights (empty: proportional to the side's bytes), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml

M3Build the Sloleks 3.2 gold, one stem-ending cut per formslm4ie/tokenizers/morphology.py::build_inflection_lexicon

Input

tokenization/sloleks_inflection.jsonl.gz, one record per lexeme (a dictionary entry with its whole paradigm) carrying its entry id, word class, manual or automatic status, and each form already cut as stem and ending, such as mačk·ah.

Output

A gold mapping each distinct form to its cut, its tag and a verified flag. It is the input of [M5].

How
  1. Every form of every lexeme is read with its cut.
  2. A form that two lexemes cut differently has no single gold cut, so it is dropped and counted ([D1]).
  3. A form with no ending is kept as one stem ([D8]).
  4. A form is verified (manual) only when every lexeme carrying it was checked by hand.
Code
slm4ie/tokenizers/morphology.py::build_inflection_lexicon
Settings
morphology.inflection_path (the converted stem-ending split), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml

M4Build the heuristic gold by aligning each form to its lemmaslm4ie/tokenizers/morphology.py::build_morph_lexicon

Input

tokenization/sloleks.jsonl.gz, one Sloleks 3.1 record per lemma (dictionary form) with its forms and their morphosyntactic tags.

Output

A gold mapping each form to a stem and a suffix, or to one whole stem. It is the reference arm of H1 and the inflectional half of the morpheme table in [M5].

How
  1. A form whose tag starts with an invariant word class (D, V, L, M, O in the Slovene tag set: preposition, conjunction, particle, interjection, abbreviation) or that holds a space is kept whole.
  2. Otherwise the cut is where the lowercased form first departs from the lowercased lemma, with rules for the usual stem changes.
  3. A form that is the lemma, or a prefix of it, is one stem. A cut shorter than min_stem_len letters is untrusted, and the form is kept whole and marked so.
  4. A form that two lemmas cut differently keeps its first cut and is counted as a collision.
Code
slm4ie/tokenizers/morphology.py::build_morph_lexicon
Settings
morphology.sloleks_path (the converted Sloleks 3.1 lexicon), morphology.min_stem_len (shortest stem trusted, 2 letters), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml

M5Hold out a fifth of the lexemes, build the morpheme table from the rest, and cut the golds to held-out formsslm4ie/tokenizers/morphology.py::split_lexemes

Input

The stem-ending split of [M3]'s input, the golds of [M3] and [M4], and the Sloleks word relations, whose derivational splits join the table.

Output

The morpheme table morph_lexicon.jsonl.gz, read by MorphBPE and MorphPiece in [M6], and the scored golds in final/morph-golds-heldout-forms/, each form with its lexeme id.

How
  1. Lexemes are grouped by word class and status. Within each group they are ordered by the hash rank of their entry id, and the lowest heldout_lexeme_share of each group is held out, so a whole paradigm sits on one side.
  2. A held-out form that a training-side lexeme also carries is dropped from scoring ([D4]).
  3. Each scored form is assigned one held-out lexeme, the unit the bootstrap resamples ([D6]). Among several carriers the lowest hash rank of form and entry id wins.
  4. The table is the derivational splits merged with the heuristic gold, minus every scored form. Training on a table that holds a scored form is refused.
  5. The golds are cut to the scored forms every gold covers.
Code
slm4ie/tokenizers/morphology.py::split_lexemes
Settings
morphology.heldout_lexeme_share (share of each group held out, 0.2), morphology.sloleks_relations_path (the word relations), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml

M6Train the six algorithms at four vocabulary sizes on the training sample, with their lineageslm4ie/tokenizers/train.py::train_sweep

Input

The training sample of [M2] and, for MorphBPE and MorphPiece, the morpheme table of [M5].

Output

One tokenizer folder per algorithm and size under final/sweep-vocab-size/<algorithm>-<size>/, with its training time and peak memory, and one MLflow child run per tokenizer.

How
  1. Each of the 24 runs trains its backend on the same training sample with the same special tokens. Unigram first cuts each document at whitespace into pieces of at most 4,192 bytes ([D13]). Character BPE, WordPiece, MorphBPE and Unigram take as base characters only those covering 99.99% of the sample's character occurrences ([D14]). The alphabet is counted once on the sample after NFC, without whitespace. The other characters leave the training text; at inference they encode as <unk>, and WordPiece turns a whole word holding one into <unk>. Byte-level BPE, character-level BPE, WordPiece and Unigram ignore the table. MorphBPE forbids merges across the table's morpheme boundaries, and MorphPiece splits table words by the table before byte-level BPE.
  2. Each run logs its algorithm, vocabulary size, the sample's seed, training seconds, and the corpus and held-out shares. The trainers themselves take no seed and are deterministic. It also logs the content hashes of the split, the training sample and the table, so a run names the exact inputs it saw.
  3. Peak memory is the highest resident memory of the training process, read once a second while the backend trains.
  4. The runs are queued MorphBPE and MorphPiece first, largest vocabulary first, so the slowest start at once.
  5. Each run carries the labflow tags tier, branch, base_commit, type and language. A tokenizer trained by a run that stopped before logging is logged by the next run that skips it.
Code
slm4ie/tokenizers/train.py::train_sweep
Settings
tokenizers (the six algorithms), vocab_sizes (16k, 32k, 64k, 128k), special_tokens (tokens reserved in every vocabulary), character_coverage (the share of character occurrences the base alphabet covers), mlflow.tags (the fixed run tags), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml

M7Score every tokenizer on the held-out forms under each gold and on both samplesexperiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/analysis.py::score_tokenizer

Input

The 24 tokenizer folders of [M6], the MorphScore v2 items and the two samples of [M2]. The scored golds of [M5] hold one row per held-out form, with the same forms in the same order under the Sloleks, heuristic and June gold.

Output

Per tokenizer, an array file with its per-form counts and a summary with Morph-Consistency, the corpus metrics, the unknown-token counts and the count bins of [D12], under the experiment's interim/tokenizer-scores/. It is the input of [M8].

How
  1. Each scored form is encoded once. Its tokens give the number of tokens and the unknown tokens among them, where an unknown token is the <unk> token or a piece outside the vocabulary.
  2. Under each gold the token boundaries inside the form are compared with the gold's, giving the counts of shared, predicted and gold boundaries. The edit distance is the number of insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn the tokens into the gold morphemes. A form whose tokens do not tile its surface text is marked invalid.
  3. Morph-Consistency is computed once on all scored forms and once on the manual ones ([D11]).
  4. Each sample is split into words, and the tokenizer encodes every distinct word once, weighted by its count. From those tokens follow fertility, tokens per byte, characters per token and the Rényi efficiency of order α, read from eval.renyi_alpha, and every vocabulary token's count, binned by scoring.count_bins ([D12]). Special tokens are left out.
  5. A tokenizer is rescored only when a digest of the golds, the samples, the settings and the scoring code changes.
Code
experiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/analysis.py::score_tokenizer
Settings
scoring.max_workers (tokenizers scored at once), scoring.count_bins (lower edges of the count bins), in configs/analysis.yaml; eval.renyi_alpha (the Rényi order), special_tokens (tokens left out of the counts), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml

M8Rank the tokenizers per gold and slice, and compute Kendall's τ with a lexeme bootstrapexperiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/analysis.py::build_scores

Input

The per-form counts of [M7] for all 24 tokenizers, each scored form's held-out lexeme from [M5], and each form's count in the evaluation sample ([D9]).

Output

The seven tables/sweep-*.csv tables and the five figures/sweep-*.svg figures the findings cite; the figures are also attached to the sweep's parent run in MLflow.

How
  1. Only forms every tokenizer tiles, meaning its tokens joined give the form back exactly, are scored ([D7]). A reading is a gold, a mask over the forms (all, manual, multi-token, with an ending, without unknown tokens, or one word class) and a per-form weight: one, or the evaluation-sample count plus one ([D9]).
  2. Per reading and tokenizer, the shared, predicted and gold boundary counts are summed per lexeme. Morpheme-boundary F1 is F1=2TP/(P+G), where TP, P and G are the summed shared, predicted and gold boundaries.
  3. Each of stats.n_resamples bootstrap draws resamples the lexemes with replacement, so a lexeme's weight is how many times it was drawn, and recomputes F1 ([D6]). The MorphScore items carry no lexeme, so they are resampled as items. Readings over the same lexemes share the draws, so both rankings of one pair come from the same resampled lexemes.
  4. Kendall's τ between two rankings is computed on the point F1 and on every paired draw; the interval is the central stats.ci_level of the draws. The 16-tokenizer readings drop the two table-trained algorithms ([D5]).
  5. Q1's rule takes, per metric, slice and algorithm, the gain from 16k to 32k and from 64k to 128k in the metric's better direction. The metric has levelled off when the late gain is under scoring.levelled_ratio of the early one, falls when it is negative, and has no early gain when the early one is not positive.
Code
experiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/analysis.py::build_scores
Settings
stats.n_resamples (bootstrap draws), stats.ci_level (central mass of each interval), stats.seed (seed of the draws), in configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml; scoring.levelled_ratio (the Q1 levelling share), scoring.rare_below (the count under which a vocabulary token is rare), in configs/analysis.yaml

Decisions

D1Score one row per distinct form and drop forms the lexicon splits two ways2026-10-22

Decision

Sloleks 3.2 repeats a form once per morphosyntactic tag; each (lexeme, form) pair is kept once. A form that two lexemes split differently is dropped from both golds. A form with no ending stays in, as a form that should not be split. A form is manual when every lexeme carrying it is manually checked.

Why

A form counted once per tag would weight long paradigms; a form with two gold cuts has no single right answer. The 74,000 forms split two ways are 2.6% of the lexicon.

History
2026-10-22 set at the start, from the scoping counts.

D2Retrain all 24 tokenizers on one new sample, with a morpheme table from the corrected heuristic2026-10-23

Decision

All six algorithms train at 16k, 32k, 64k and 128k on the training sample of the corpus split ([D3]). MorphBPE and MorphPiece use one morpheme table: the corrected heuristic's cuts plus the word-relation splits, with every scored form removed ([D4]).

Why

The June sample came from an earlier corpus build, so the June tokenizers cannot join a sweep on the current one. The corrected heuristic is the morphological algorithms' own method with its bug fixed; a table from the Sloleks split is a method change, planned as its own experiment.

Alternatives
  • Reuse the 18 June tokenizers and train only 128k: they were trained on an older corpus.
  • Build the table from the Sloleks split: favours the Sloleks gold by construction.
History
2026-10-23 worded as built before any run: the table removes the scored forms, not whole lexemes, so it keeps Sloleks 3.1 forms that 3.2 lacks.

D3Split the corpus 80/20 by document within each source, and sample each side in proportion to its sources2026-10-23

Decision

Each document is ranked by a hash of its source and id; within each source, the lowest 80% go to training and the rest to evaluation. A 2 GB training sample and a 200 MB evaluation sample are drawn from the two sides, each source taking its share of that side's bytes.

Why

Exact per-source proportions keep small sources on both sides. A held-out side means no evaluated document was seen in training, by id. The same text under two ids can still sit on both sides; the data review found 34 such lines in the training sample. A hash rank is reproducible without storing 30 million ids.

Alternatives
  • Split one 2.5 GB sample: the evaluation side would be one small draw, not reusable.
  • Weight sources equally, as the June sampler did: a 367-document source would weigh as much as the largest web crawl.
History
2026-10-23 worded as built before any run: the source shares are by bytes, as the sampler draws them.

D4Split the lexemes 80/20 within each word class and status, and score only held-out forms2026-10-22

Decision

Sloleks 3.2 lexemes are split 80/20 by a hash of their id, exactly within each word class and checking status. A held-out form that also occurs in a training lexeme is dropped from scoring. The morpheme table drops every scored form, and keeps the forms a training lexeme shares with a held-out one.

Why

MorphPiece emits the table's cuts for words it knows and MorphBPE trains on them, so a form in the table is scored on memory. Splitting lexemes, not forms, keeps the whole paradigm on one side. Published form-level splits leak: 69% of SIGMORPHON 2022 English inflected test words have their base in training.

Alternatives
  • Split by form, as SIGMORPHON 2022 and MorphBPE do: forms of one paradigm land on both sides.
History
2026-10-22 table rule worded as built, before any run: the table keeps shared forms, which are never scored.

D5Report the rank agreements also without the two algorithms that train on a morpheme table2026-10-22

Decision

Beside H1 and H2 on all 24 tokenizers, τ is reported on the 16 tokenizers of BPE, character BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Why

With held-out lexemes no form is memorised, but the table still teaches heuristic-style endings, which may favour the heuristic gold. If the two readings differ, the table explains the difference rather than the gold.

History
2026-10-22 set with the user before any run.

D6Resample lexemes, not forms, for every bootstrap interval on the morph metrics2026-10-22

Decision

Per-form counts are summed per held-out lexeme, and each bootstrap draw resamples lexemes. A form carried by two held-out lexemes counts under the one its hash picks. The intervals on τ for H1 and H2 come from these draws.

Why

The forms of one paradigm share a stem and are cut alike, so they are not independent. Resampling about half a million forms would give an interval too narrow to straddle a bar.

Alternatives
  • Resample forms, as the code did: treats correlated forms as independent and overstates certainty.
History
2026-10-22 set with the user before any run, after a literature comparison.

D7Score every tokenizer on all held-out forms, including those it keeps as one token2026-10-22

Decision

The primary score counts a form the tokenizer leaves whole as one with its gold boundary missed. Morpheme-boundary F1 on multi-token forms only is read beside the clauses.

Why

Τ needs every tokenizer ranked on the same forms. At 128k many frequent forms are one token, so the beside reading separates boundary placement from vocabulary coverage.

Alternatives
  • Exclude one-token forms, as MorphScore v1 does: each tokenizer is then scored on its own subset.
  • Keep only forms whose gold pieces are vocabulary entries, as Uzan et al. and FLOTA do: also per-tokenizer subsets.
History
2026-10-22 set with the user before any run, after a literature comparison.

D8Keep forms with no ending, and read the score without them beside the clauses2026-10-22

Decision

A form whose gold has no ending stays in the scored set as a form that should not be split ([D1]). Morpheme-boundary F1 without these forms is read beside the clauses.

Why

Splitting such a form is a real tokenizer fault, and these forms only lower precision. The beside reading shows whether over-splitting moves the ranking.

Alternatives
  • Drop them, as MorphScore v2 and Bostrom & Durrett do: precision would then ignore over-splitting.
History
2026-10-22 set with the user before any run, after a literature comparison.

D9Read a frequency-weighted morpheme-boundary F1 beside the type-level clauses2026-10-22

Decision

Each held-out form is weighted by its count in the evaluation sample plus one ([D3]). A counted word is a maximal run of letters, matched to the form lowercased; forms that differ only in case share a count. The weighted F1 is read beside the clauses; H1, H2 and Q1 stay on the unweighted, one-count-per-form score.

Why

BPE-knockout and Bostrom & Durrett weight by corpus frequency, and the weighted score reacts to leakage very differently from the type-level one. The add-one keeps forms absent from the sample.

Alternatives
  • Read H1 on the weighted score too: doubles the verdict surface for a score dominated by short frequent forms.
History
2026-10-22 set with the user before any run, after a literature comparison.

D10Score the tokenizers without a morpheme table on the MorphScore v2 Slovene set as an outside gold2026-10-22

Decision

The 16 tokenizers of [D5] are scored on the MorphScore v2 Slovene items, and τ between that ranking and the Sloleks 3.2 ranking is read beside the clauses.

Why

The set is cut by a different method from different text, so agreement shows the ranking is not a Sloleks artefact. Its lemmas were never held out, so the two table algorithms could score on memory.

Alternatives
  • Score all 24 on the items whose lemma is a held-out lexeme: keeps every algorithm, leaves about a fifth of the items.
History
2026-10-22 set with the user before any run, after a literature comparison.

D11Draw Morph-Consistency pairs from each shared morpheme, at most 200 pairs per morpheme2026-10-22

Decision

Morph-Consistency pairs every two scored forms that share a gold morpheme or a token, capped at 200 sampled pairs per morpheme or token. It is a point estimate with no interval.

Why

On a stem-ending gold a shared morpheme is a stem or an ending. A few hundred endings give few pairs and about 100,000 stems give many, so the score mostly asks whether a paradigm keeps its stem token.

Alternatives
  • MorphBPE's k-means sampling, 50 pairs per cluster: its clusters have no clear meaning on a two-morpheme gold.
  • Separate stem and ending consistency: one more metric for a secondary reading.
History
2026-10-22 set with the user before any run, after a literature comparison.

D12Count how often each vocabulary token occurs in both samples, and read the rare share beside Q12026-10-23

Decision

Each of the 24 tokenizers encodes both samples ([D3]) and counts every vocabulary token per sample. A table per tokenizer and sample puts the vocabulary in the count bins 0, 1–9, 10–99, 100–999 and 1,000 or more. Each bin shows its share of the vocabulary and of the sample's tokens. The rare share is read beside Q1.

Why

A token seen only a few times gives a language model too few examples to learn its embedding. A 128k vocabulary that gains on the morph metrics but holds many such tokens may still be the worse choice for a small model. Counts per million tokens carry the reading to a pretraining corpus of any size.

Alternatives
  • A bar on the rare share: no level can be set before the counts exist, so it stays a reading.
  • Count on the whole training side of the corpus: ten times the encoding cost for counts the per-million scale already gives.
History
2026-10-23 set with the user before any run.

D13Cut each document into pieces SentencePiece accepts before Unigram trains on it2026-10-23

Decision

Unigram trains on every document, cut at whitespace into pieces of at most 4,192 bytes. The other five algorithms read whole documents.

Why

SentencePiece drops any line longer than 4,192 bytes, and the sample holds one document per line. Uncut, Unigram would train on 41% of the sample's bytes, mostly short documents with a different source mix. The June Unigram tokenizers had this loss, so their scores are not comparable.

Alternatives
  • Raise SentencePiece's line limit: long lines strain its memory, and a cut at a space loses only cross-piece pairs.
History
2026-10-23 set before any run, after the pre-launch review measured the loss.

D14Give the character-level algorithms only the characters that cover 99.99% of the sample2026-10-23

Decision

Character BPE, WordPiece, MorphBPE and Unigram take as base characters the most frequent ones that together cover 99.99% of the training sample's character occurrences: the same 236 of 6,074 for all four. The other characters encode as <unk>. Unigram gets this alphabet, not SentencePiece's own coverage, which counts spaces and NFKC forms. Byte-level BPE and MorphPiece keep their 256 bytes.

Why

With every character kept, 5,369 of Unigram's 16,000 pieces were single characters, mostly other scripts, private-use and mis-decoded text. The byte-level algorithms pay no such cost, so the 16k ranking would partly measure the alphabet. At 99.95%, SentencePiece's default, ü, ö, á, đ and Ć drop out and 0.98% of the Sloleks forms hold one; at 99.99%, 0.057% do.

Alternatives
  • Keep every character, as the libraries do by default: a third of a 16k vocabulary goes to single characters.
  • Cover 99.95%: drops letters of names the gold scores.
  • Clean the corpus first: a curation rebuild of several days, planned on its own.
History
2026-10-23 set with the user before any tracked run, after the smoke run counted the single-character pieces. 99.99% was chosen over the proposed 99.95% after counting the forms each drops.

Reproduce

The Sloleks 3.2 file sits at data/raw/sloleks/Sloleks 3.2/DSBS__inflect_morph_seg__2026-07.tsv, placed by hand, and the curated corpus at data/pretrain/06_sentence_dedup/. The lexicon conversions sloleks, sloleks_inflection, sloleks_relations and morphscore_slovenian from configs/data/tokenization.yaml must exist under data/tokenization/.

  1. env
    export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:5555   # the shared server
cd <repo>   # with data/ linked to /vault/data/SLM4IE
  2. 1
    Corpus split, both samples and the morpheme table (commit cd57bce)
    uv run python scripts/sweep_tokenizers.py sample --config experiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml --max-workers 4
  3. 2
    Scored golds, held-out form counts, MorphScore items and the dataset tables (commit cd57bce)
    uv run --group analysis python experiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/analysis.py data
  4. 3
    [F1] to [F6] — train the 24 tokenizers, tracked (commit 7d81996)
    uv run python scripts/sweep_tokenizers.py train --config experiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/configs/sweep-vocab-size.yaml --all --tier tracked --max-workers 4
  5. 4
    [F1] to [F6] — score and rank the tokenizers, and draw every table and figure (commit 8f408e8)
    uv run --group analysis python experiments/validation/morph-gold-slovenian/analysis.py scores

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/README.md

Encoder Transformers

open6 entries0 checked

Which encoder design should a small Slovenian model for information extraction be built on, and which of its parts can be swapped without changing the rest?

An encoder Transformer reads a whole text at once and gives every token one vector that reflects the tokens on both sides of it. Information extraction reads such vectors directly: a named entity is a span whose tokens are tagged, and a relation is a pair of spans. The entries here are the lineage that runs from BERT to the encoders released in 2024. Each one keeps most of its predecessor and changes a few parts: how position is told to the model, how far a token can attend, where the normalisation sits inside a block, which activation the feed-forward part uses, and what the model is trained to predict. The Compared table shows those parts side by side, so an experiment can name the one it varies.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/bert.md

BERT

from paperin topic Encoder TransformersarXiv:1810.04805arXiv:1706.03762
In one lineA stack of Transformer encoder layers over token, segment and learned absolute position embeddings, pretrained to recover 15% masked tokens and to tell whether two segments were adjacent.
DescriptionAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

BERT is an encoder: it reads a whole text at once and gives every token one vector that depends on the tokens to its left and to its right. The model is a stack of identical Transformer layers. Each layer lets every token gather information from every other token through attention, then passes the result through a small feed-forward network. Position is told to the model only once, at the input, by adding a learned vector for each of the 512 positions to the token's embedding.

  • Pretraining teaches the encoder two things. Masked language modelling hides 15% of the tokens and asks the model to name them from the rest of the text. Next-sentence prediction shows the model two segments and asks whether the second followed the first in the source document.
  • Fine-tuning adds one layer on top. For a tagging task such as named entity recognition, a linear layer over every token vector gives the tag. For a sentence task, the vector of the leading [CLS] token stands for the whole input.
  • Two sizes were released. Base has 12 layers of width 768 with 12 attention heads and 110M parameters. Large has 24 layers of width 1024 with 16 heads and 340M parameters.

What the paper adds

Before BERT, pretrained language models read text in one direction, so a token's vector could only see what came before it. The paper's claim is that masking makes a bidirectional encoder trainable: the model cannot cheat by copying the token it is asked to predict, because the token is hidden. The paper also fixes the input convention that later encoders kept, a [CLS] token in front, a [SEP] token between segments, and a segment embedding that tells the two apart.

Why it matters here

Every encoder in this topic is a change to BERT, and the Slovenian encoders that benchmark results are usually reported with, CroSloEngual BERT and the multilingual BERT, are BERT itself trained on other text. An information extraction model that tags spans reads the per-token vectors BERT produces, so BERT is the baseline design any small Slovenian encoder is measured against.

Facts

Position encodinglearned absolute, one vector per position added to the token embedding at the input, 512 positions
Attention spanevery token attends to every token of the input
Block normalisationpost-norm, a layer norm after each of the two residual additions
ActivationGELU in a feed-forward network of inner width four times the hidden width
Pretraining objectivemasked language modelling on 15% of the tokens, plus next-sentence prediction
TokenizerWordPiece, 30,000 pieces
Context length512 tokens
Input[CLS], segment A, [SEP], segment B, [SEP], with a learned segment embedding for A and for B
SizesBase 12 layers, width 768, 12 heads, 110M parameters; Large 24 layers, width 1024, 16 heads, 340M parameters
Maskingof the 15% chosen positions, 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token, 10% stay unchanged
Training dataBooksCorpus, 800M words, and English Wikipedia, 2,500M words
OptimizerAdam, learning rate 1e-4, warmup over 10,000 steps then linear decay, weight decay 0.01, dropout 0.1
Training length1,000,000 steps of 256 sequences, about 40 passes over the data, 90% of the steps at length 128 and the last 10% at 512
Prediction heada dense layer with GELU and layer norm, then a softmax over the vocabulary whose weights are the input embeddings

Sources

Paper
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding, Devlin et al., NAACL 2019, arXiv:1810.04805
Attention Is All You Need, Vaswani et al., NeurIPS 2017, arXiv:1706.03762, the encoder layer BERT stacks
Code

Example

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. BERT encoder: from token ids to one vector per token

Require: token ids x1,…,xn with n≤512, segment ids si∈{A,B}, embedding tables Etok, Eseg, Epos, L layers of width d with A heads

Ensure: hidden states h1L,…,hnL

  1. hi0←Dropout(LN(Etok[xi]+Eseg[si]+Epos[i])) for every i
  2. for ℓ=1,…,L do
  3. a← multi-head attention over hℓ−1 with A heads: for each head, softmaxj(qi·kj/d/A)vj summed over all j
  4. u←LN(hℓ−1+Dropout(Woa))
  5. f←W2GELU(W1u+b1)+b2 with inner width 4d
  6. hℓ←LN(u+Dropout(f))
  7. return hL

Reading Algorithm 1

1Each token starts as the sum of three learned vectors: what the token is, which of the two segments it belongs to, and where it stands. The sum passes through a layer norm, which rescales every vector to a fixed spread. Position enters only here, so a later layer knows where a token is only through what this sum carried.2–3Every layer begins with attention. A token builds a query from its own vector and compares it with a key built from every other token, so the weights say how much each token matters to it. The weighted sum of value vectors is what the token gathers. The division by the square root of the head width keeps the comparisons from growing with the width.4The gathered information is added back to the token's own vector, and the sum is normalised. The norm sits after the addition, which is the post-norm arrangement.5–6A feed-forward network, the same for every token, widens the vector four times, applies the GELU activation and narrows it back. Its output is added to the token's vector and normalised again. This is where most of the model's parameters sit.7After the last layer every token has a vector that reflects the whole input. A tagging model reads these vectors one by one.

Algorithm 2. BERT pretraining example: masked language modelling with next-sentence prediction

Require: a corpus of documents split into sentences, WordPiece vocabulary V, maximum length T=512

Ensure: one input sequence, its masked-token targets and its next-sentence label

  1. draw a run of sentences A from one document; with probability 0.5 let B be the sentences that follow A (label IsNext), otherwise sentences drawn from another document (label NotNext); trim so that |A|+|B|≤T−3
  2. x← [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP], with segment id A for the first part and B for the second
  3. M← 15% of the token positions of x, drawn at random once, excluding the three special tokens
  4. for all i∈M do
  5. with probability 0.8 replace xi by [MASK]; with 0.1 by a random token of V; with 0.1 keep xi
  6. h← Algorithm 1 on x
  7. LMLM←∑i∈M cross-entropy of softmax(EtokLN(GELU(Whi))+b) against the original xi
  8. LNSP← cross-entropy of a two-way classifier on tanh(Wph1) against the label
  9. return LMLM+LNSP

Reading Algorithm 2

1Half of the examples pair a segment with its true continuation, half with text from elsewhere. The label is what next-sentence prediction has to recover. The two segments together fill the 512 positions, minus the three special tokens.2The two segments are laid out with the special tokens between them. The segment ids are the only thing that tells the model where A ends and B begins, besides the separator.3–5The positions to hide are chosen once per example, when the corpus is prepared, and the same mask is reused on every pass over the data. Most hidden positions get the [MASK] token. One in ten gets a random token, and one in ten is left as it is, so that the model cannot assume an unmasked token is right and keeps a useful vector for every position. [MASK] never appears in fine-tuning, which is the mismatch the two smaller cases soften.6The encoder of Algorithm 1 runs over the corrupted sequence.7Only the chosen positions are scored. The head transforms the token vector once more and scores it against the input embedding table, so the output and input vocabularies share one set of vectors.8The vector of the leading [CLS] token is passed through a small pooling layer and a two-way classifier that says IsNext or NotNext.9The two losses are added with equal weight.

Worked example

The topic's example script holds no BERT example. BERT's two mechanisms that later entries change, the absolute position table and the fixed mask, have nothing to compute: the position of token i is row i of the table, and the mask is a draw. The DeBERTa V2 entry shows the table that replaces the first, and the RoBERTa entry explains what replaces the second.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Position is told once and absolutely

The model learns one vector per position and never sees the distance between two tokens directly. A pattern learned at positions 10 and 12 has to be learned again at 300 and 302, and no input can be longer than the 512 rows of the table.

The mask is fixed when the corpus is prepared

Every pass over the data hides the same tokens of the same sentence, so forty passes give forty views of one masking. RoBERTa draws the mask anew each time.

Next-sentence prediction costs half the input

Half of the examples pair a segment with unrelated text, so the second half of those inputs teaches the encoder little about language. RoBERTa measured no loss from dropping the task.

The [MASK] token is never seen downstream

Pretraining sees [MASK] at 12% of the positions and fine-tuning never does, so the model is trained on an input distribution it will not meet. The 10% random and 10% unchanged cases reduce the mismatch but do not remove it.

Short training at full length

Nine tenths of the steps run on sequences of 128 tokens, so the position vectors for positions 129 to 512 are trained on one tenth of the data.

Related

Couples toWordPieceCharacter BPE training with a marker on every character inside a word, keeping only the vocabulary; a new word is cut by taking the longest piece in the vocabulary from each position.VariantRoBERTaBERT's encoder unchanged, retrained with a fresh mask on every pass, full sentences packed across document boundaries, no next-sentence prediction, a byte-level BPE vocabulary, and ten times the data at a batch of 8,000 sequences.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/deberta-v2.md

DeBERTa V2

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of DeBERTaarXiv:2006.03654arXiv:2111.09543arXiv:1910.10683
In one lineDeBERTa with a 128,000-piece SentencePiece vocabulary learned on the training data, relative distances compressed onto log-spaced buckets, position projections shared with the content projections, and a convolution beside the first layer.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

DeBERTa V2 is the architecture the 900M and 1.5B DeBERTa models were trained with, released with the authors' code rather than a paper of its own. It keeps disentangled attention and the enhanced mask decoder and changes four things around them.

  • A larger vocabulary, learned on the training data. 128,000 pieces from SentencePiece replace the 50,000 pieces of GPT-2's byte-level BPE. The embedding table grows to almost half the parameters of the base model.
  • Relative distances are bucketed. Distances up to 128 either way keep a row each. Longer distances share rows spaced on a log scale, up to 255 rows each way, so 512 rows cover what V1 covered with 1,024 and a longer input still finds a row.
  • The position projections are the content projections. The query and key matrices that V1 kept apart for the relative position table are the ones used for content, which removes two matrices per layer.
  • A convolution beside the first layer. A one-dimensional convolution of width three over the input embeddings is added to the output of the first Transformer layer, so that the first layer's output carries the three-token neighbourhood of every token directly. The authors call this n-gram induced input encoding, nGiE.

What the paper adds

There is no V2 paper. The DeBERTa paper's section on the 1.5B model describes the shared projections and the convolution with an ablation on base models showing the sharing costs no accuracy. The repository's release notes add the vocabulary and the buckets. The DeBERTa V3 paper names V2 as the architecture it inherits.

Why it matters here

Two of V2's changes are the ones a Slovenian model would weigh first. The vocabulary is learned on the training text with SentencePiece, which is the Unigram model of this project's tokenizer sweep, so a Slovenian vocabulary drops in without changing the encoder. The bucketed distances are what makes a context past 512 tokens possible for the disentangled design. The convolution is a cheap way to give the first layer the character of a three-token window, which for an inflected language puts a word and its neighbours' endings together.

Facts

Position encodingrelative, bucketed; distances up to 128 keep their own row, longer ones share rows on a log scale, 512 rows in all; absolute position added before the masked-token prediction only
Attention spanevery token attends to every token, as in BERT
Block normalisationpost-norm, as in BERT, with a layer norm on the relative position table
ActivationGELU, as in BERT
Pretraining objectivemasked language modelling on 15% of the tokens, as in RoBERTa
TokenizerSentencePiece, 128,000 pieces learned on the training data
Context length512 tokens in training; the bucketed table reaches any distance
Position buckets256 per side; the scale is stretched so that distance 511 reaches the last bucket
Projectionsthe query and key matrices of the content are applied to the relative position table too
Convolutionkernel 3 over the input embeddings, GELU, added to the first layer's output and normalised; released in the XLarge and XXLarge models
SizesXLarge 24 layers, width 1536, 24 heads, 710M parameters; XXLarge 48 layers, width 1536, 24 heads, 1.32B parameters
Training data160GB, the RoBERTa sources
Optimizeras in DeBERTa

Sources

Paper
DeBERTa: Decoding-enhanced BERT with Disentangled Attention, He, Liu, Gao and Chen, ICLR 2021, arXiv:2006.03654, section 5.1 and appendix on the 1.5B model, for the shared projections and the convolution
DeBERTaV3: Improving DeBERTa using ELECTRA-Style Pre-Training with Gradient-Disentangled Embedding Sharing, He, Gao and Chen, ICLR 2023, arXiv:2111.09543, section 4, for the vocabulary and data V2 and V3 share
Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer, Raffel et al., 2020, arXiv:1910.10683, whose log-spaced relative position buckets V2 adopts
Code
none in this repository; the reference implementation is the DebertaV2Model of the HuggingFace transformers library, whose make_log_bucket_position the example script ports
Example
experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/examples.py
Paper vs code
the release notes say "log bucket similar to T5". The released code keeps exact distances up to half the bucket count and places the rest with ⌈log(|r|/128)/log(511/128)·127⌉+128, which the worked example computes. T5 uses a fixed number of exact buckets and a different scale.

Difference from predecessor

Against DeBERTa: log-bucketed relative distances, shared position projections, a convolution beside the first layer, and a 128,000-piece SentencePiece vocabulary.

DeBERTa2, 3 and the first layer of Algorithm 1 of DeBERTa:the position table has 2k=1024 rows, each distance up to 512 its own row, projected by its own query and key matrices; the first layer is a plain Transformer layer
DeBERTa V22, 3 and the first layer of Algorithm 1 of DeBERTa:512 rows reached through log-spaced buckets, projected by the content's own matrices; a width-three convolution of the input embeddings is added to the first layer's output

Effect. Any distance finds a row at half the table size, two projections per layer disappear, and the first layer sees every token's three-token neighbourhood.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. DeBERTa V2 encoder: convolution beside the first layer and bucketed relative attention

Require: token ids x1,…,xn, embedding table Etok, relative position table P∈ℝ2b×d with b=256 buckets per side, stretch k=512, L layers whose attention follows DeBERTa Algorithm 1 with the changes below

Ensure: hidden states hL

  1. h0←LN(Etok[x])
  2. h1←LN(layer1(h0)+GELU(Conv3(h0)))
  3. for ℓ=2,…,L do
  4. Qr←LN(P)Wq,c, Kr←LN(P)Wk,c, with the content's own matrices of layer ℓ
  5. r←i−j, m←b/2; β(r)←r if |r|≤m, else sign(r)·(⌈log(|r|/m)/log((k−1)/m)·(m−1)⌉+m)
  6. δ(i,j)←β(i−j)+b, clamped to [0,2b−1]
  7. hℓ← DeBERTa Algorithm 1 with these Qr, Kr and δ, then residual, norm and feed-forward as in BERT
  8. return hL

Reading Algorithm 1

1As in DeBERTa, the token embedding enters alone and no position is added at the input.2The first layer runs as in DeBERTa. Beside it a convolution of kernel three slides over the input embeddings, so each output mixes a token with its left and right neighbour. The two results are added and normalised together. The convolution runs on the input only, so layers 2 to L do not have it.3–4In every layer the relative position table is first normalised and then projected by the same query and key matrices the layer uses for content. The two position-only matrices of DeBERTa are gone.5A distance of 128 or less is its own bucket. A longer distance is mapped onto a log scale that reaches bucket 255 at distance 511, so distances from 129 to 511 share 127 buckets, with a bucket covering more distances the further out it lies. The sign is kept, so left and right neighbours never share a row.6The bucket is shifted by b to index the table, and clamped, so a distance beyond 511 reads the outermost row rather than failing.7–8The attention itself is DeBERTa's three-term score with the scale 3d, and everything after it is BERT's layer.

Worked example

The example script ports the bucket rule of the released code to plain Python and applies it to a set of distances, next to the row DeBERTa V1 would read with k=512. The last column counts how many distances from 0 to 511 land in the same row.

Up to distance 128 the two agree except for the offset of the table. From 129 on, V2 starts merging: 150 lands in bucket 143, 200 in 169 with two neighbours, and 400 in 233 with four. V1 keeps every distance up to 511 apart and sends 512, 600 and 1000 to the same outer row. V2 sends them to its outer row too, since the table ends at bucket 255, but a model trained with a stretch k larger than 512 would keep them apart.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The convolution is a release detail

The released base and large V3 models carry no convolution, only the V2 XLarge and XXLarge do. Which sizes it helps is not reported.

Half the parameters of a small model are embeddings

At width 768 the 128,000-piece table holds 98M parameters against 86M in the layers. A small Slovenian model would set the vocabulary size by the tokenizer sweep, not by this release.

Long distances share a row from 129 on

A bucket near 400 covers five distances, so two tokens 398 and 402 apart look the same to the position side. What this costs at a context of 512 is not measured; it is the price of reaching beyond.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/deberta-v3.md

DeBERTa V3

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of DeBERTa V2arXiv:2111.09543arXiv:2003.10555
In one lineDeBERTa V2 trained as the discriminator of replaced token detection, with a half-depth generator whose token embeddings it shares while its own gradient is kept from them.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

DeBERTa V3 keeps the V2 encoder and changes what it is trained to do. Instead of predicting masked tokens, the encoder is trained as a discriminator: a smaller generator fills the masked positions with plausible tokens, and the discriminator says, for every position, whether the token there is the original or a replacement. This is the replaced token detection of ELECTRA. The encoder learns from every position rather than from the 15% that were masked.

  • Two models train side by side. The generator is a V2 encoder of the same width and half the depth, trained with masked language modelling. The discriminator is the full V2 encoder with a two-way classifier on every token. Only the discriminator is kept.
  • Token embeddings are shared with a one-way gradient. The discriminator uses the generator's embedding table plus a residual table of its own. The generator's table is updated by the masked-token loss only. The residual table is updated by the detection loss only. After training the two tables are added and saved as the discriminator's.
  • Everything else is V2. Disentangled attention with bucketed distances, shared projections, the 128,000-piece SentencePiece vocabulary, and the 160GB RoBERTa data. The released base and large models carry no convolution.

What the paper adds

The paper's diagnosis is a tug of war. In ELECTRA the two models share one embedding table, and the two losses pull it in opposite directions: masked language modelling draws similar tokens together, detection pushes them apart to make replacements easier to spot. Separate tables train faster but give a worse discriminator, because the generator's embeddings are the better ones. Gradient-disentangled embedding sharing keeps the generator's table as the base and lets the discriminator add only a correction, which the paper shows trains as fast as separate tables and scores higher than either.

Why it matters here

Replaced token detection is the training objective that lets a small encoder make the most of a small corpus, since every token of every sequence yields a training signal. For Slovenian, where the corpus is a hundredth of what the English models saw, that is the lever this entry offers. The objective is independent of the encoder's layers, so it can be paired with any entry of this topic, and an experiment that varies the objective would name this entry.

Facts

Position encodingrelative, bucketed, as in DeBERTa V2
Attention spanevery token attends to every token, as in BERT
Block normalisationpost-norm, as in BERT
ActivationGELU, as in BERT
Pretraining objectivereplaced token detection; a generator trained with masked language modelling on 15% of the tokens fills the masks, the discriminator classifies every token as original or replaced, loss LMLM+50LRTD
TokenizerSentencePiece, 128,000 pieces, the DeBERTa V2 vocabulary; mDeBERTa uses 250,000 pieces
Context length512 tokens
Generatorsame width as the discriminator, half its depth
Embedding sharingthe discriminator's table is the generator's, with the gradient stopped, plus a residual table started at zero; after training the two are added and saved
SizesBase 12 layers, width 768, 86M backbone and 98M embedding parameters; Large 24 layers, width 1024, 304M backbone; Small 6 layers, width 768, 44M; XSmall 12 layers, width 384, 22M
Training data160GB, the RoBERTa sources; mDeBERTa on the 2.5TB CC100 multilingual corpus
OptimizerAdamW with β1=0.9, β2=0.98, learning rate 6e-4 for Base and Small and 3e-4 for Large, warmup over 10,000 steps, linear decay
Training length500,000 steps of 8,192 sequences
Convolutionnone in the released base and large models

Difference from predecessor

Against DeBERTa V2: replaced token detection in place of masked language modelling, with gradient-disentangled embedding sharing.

DeBERTa V2Algorithm 2 of RoBERTa's lineage, the pretraining step, against Algorithm 1 here:one encoder, trained to name the 15% masked tokens
DeBERTa V3Algorithm 2 of RoBERTa's lineage, the pretraining step, against Algorithm 1 here:a half-depth generator names the masked tokens and fills them in; the encoder is trained to tell original tokens from the replacements, at every position, with a shared embedding table whose gradient flows one way

Effect. Every token of every sequence trains the encoder, and the embedding table is shaped by the generator alone with a correction learned by the discriminator.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. One training step of replaced token detection with gradient-disentangled embedding sharing

Require: a sequence x of n tokens, generator G with parameters θG and embedding table EG, discriminator D with parameters θD and residual embedding table EΔ started at zero, weight λ=50

Ensure: updated θG, EG, θD, EΔ

  1. x~G←x with 15% of its positions M masked, replaced as in BERT
  2. LMLM←∑i∈M cross-entropy of G(x~G)i against xi
  3. update θG and EG by the gradient of LMLM
  4. x~D←x with each xi, i∈M, replaced by a token sampled from the distribution G(x~G)i, without gradient
  5. ED←sg(EG)+EΔ
  6. LRTD←∑i=1n binary cross-entropy of D(x~D)i against 1[x~D,i≠xi], with D embedding its input through ED
  7. update θD and EΔ by the gradient of λLRTD
  8. return after the last step, save EG+EΔ as the discriminator's embedding table

Reading Algorithm 1

1–2The generator sees BERT's corrupted input and is scored as BERT is, on the masked positions only. It is a V2 encoder of half the depth with the usual prediction head.3The generator and its embedding table learn from the masked-token loss alone. This is the step that, in ELECTRA, also received the detection gradient.4The discriminator's input is the original sequence with the masked positions filled by what the generator proposes. A proposal that happens to equal the original counts as original. Sampling is detached, so no gradient flows from the discriminator into the generator through the tokens.5The discriminator's embedding table is the generator's, read through a stop-gradient so that its own loss cannot change it, plus a residual table of its own. At the first step the residual is zero and the two models embed tokens identically.6Every position is scored, not only the masked ones. The label is whether the token differs from the original. A sequence of 512 tokens gives 512 training signals where masked language modelling gives about 77.7The detection loss, weighted by 50 as in ELECTRA, updates the discriminator's layers and the residual embedding table. The generator's table receives nothing from it, which is what breaks the tug of war.8What is released is the discriminator with one embedding table, the sum of the two, so a downstream user sees an ordinary encoder.

Worked example

The topic's example script holds no V3 example. The training step has no rule to tabulate: its inputs are draws from the generator, and its effect is in the trained weights.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Two encoders in memory during training

The generator adds half an encoder's layers and a second forward pass per step. The paper counts the cost of a step as the same across sharing methods, but it is higher than masked language modelling alone.

The weight 50 is inherited

λ=50 is ELECTRA's value, taken over without a sweep. Whether a smaller model or a smaller corpus wants another weight is not reported.

Masked language modelling is lost as a probe

The released discriminator cannot fill in a blank, so a zero-shot use that asks the model to name a masked word, which a masked language model can do, is not available from this encoder.

A generator the same width as a small model

For a small discriminator the half-depth generator is still a sizeable model, and ELECTRA found that a generator too strong for its discriminator hurts. The paper reports base and larger, not what happens below XSmall.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/deberta.md

DeBERTa

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of RoBERTaarXiv:2006.03654arXiv:1803.02155
In one lineRoBERTa's recipe with attention that scores content and relative position separately, no position at the input, and absolute position added only in the last layers before the masked-token prediction.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

DeBERTa keeps RoBERTa's data, vocabulary and training recipe and changes how the encoder handles position. In BERT and RoBERTa a token's vector is the sum of what it is and where it is, and attention compares those sums. DeBERTa keeps the two apart. Every token has a content vector, and every pair of tokens has a relative position vector that depends only on how far apart they are. Attention adds up three comparisons: content against content, content against the other token's relative position, and this token's relative position against the other's content.

  • Position is not added at the input. The token embedding enters the first layer alone. Distance between tokens is read inside every layer from a shared table of relative position vectors with one row per distance up to 512 either way.
  • Absolute position is added at the end. Where a token stands in the sentence still matters for predicting a masked word, so the model adds the absolute position vectors to the states after the second-to-last layer and runs the last layer twice on that sum. The paper calls this the enhanced mask decoder.
  • Fine-tuning can add scale-invariant perturbation. SiFT, used only for the 1.5B model, normalises the word embeddings before adding the adversarial noise of virtual adversarial training, so the noise is the same size for every token.

What the paper adds

The paper argues that the position-to-content term, which earlier relative position schemes dropped, matters: how much a token attends to a neighbour depends on their distance and on which of the two carries the content. It shows by ablation that removing either position term or the enhanced mask decoder costs accuracy on every benchmark measured. The 1.5B-parameter model was the first to pass the human baseline on SuperGLUE.

Why it matters here

Slovenian word order is freer than English word order, and the case endings carry what the position carries in English. An encoder that reads distance rather than absolute place is a plausible fit for that, and this is the first design in the lineage that does so. The relative position table is also the part a small model can shrink or share across layers without touching the rest. DeBERTa's released vocabulary is RoBERTa's byte-level BPE, so the tokenizer finding carries over.

Difference from predecessor

Against RoBERTa: disentangled attention over content and relative position, with absolute position moved from the input to the decoder.

RoBERTa1 of BERT's Algorithm 1 and line 3 of it, against Algorithm 1 here:the token embedding, the segment embedding and the absolute position embedding are summed at the input, and attention compares those sums
DeBERTa1 of BERT's Algorithm 1 and line 3 of it, against Algorithm 1 here:the token embedding enters alone; attention adds a content-to-content, a content-to-position and a position-to-content score read from a shared table of relative distances; absolute position is added before the prediction head

Effect. Every layer reads how far two tokens are apart, and where a token stands is used only to predict the masked word.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. Disentangled self-attention in one layer, one head

Require: content states H∈ℝn×d, relative position table P∈ℝ2k×d shared by all layers with k=512, content projections Wq,c,Wk,c,Wv,c, position projections Wq,r,Wk,r

Ensure: attention output Ho∈ℝn×d

  1. Qc←HWq,c, Kc←HWk,c, Vc←HWv,c
  2. Qr←PWq,r, Kr←PWk,r
  3. δ(i,j)←0 if i−j≤−k; 2k−1 if i−j≥k; i−j+k otherwise
  4. A~ij←Qc,iKc,j⊤+Qc,iKr,δ(i,j)⊤+Kc,jQr,δ(j,i)⊤ for every i,j
  5. Ho←softmax(A~/3d)Vc
  6. return Ho

Reading Algorithm 1

1The content side is BERT's attention: a query, a key and a value for every token, from its content vector alone.2The position side projects the shared table once per layer. Row r of Qr and Kr stands for the signed distance r−k, so the table holds every distance from −k to k−1. It is one table for the whole model, and each layer applies its own projections to it.3The signed distance from token i to token j is turned into a row index. Distances beyond k either way share the two outer rows.4Three scores are added. The first asks how well the content of j answers the content of i. The second asks how well the distance to j answers the content of i. The third asks how well the content of j answers the distance from j back to i, which is why its index is δ(j,i). The fourth possible term, position against position, is left out because a distance compared with itself carries nothing.5The sum of three dot products has three times the spread of one, so the scale is 3d rather than BERT's d. The paper reports this factor matters for stable training of large models.6The output has the same shape as BERT's and feeds the same residual, norm and feed-forward steps.

Algorithm 2. Masked language modelling with the enhanced mask decoder

Require: corrupted token ids x with masked positions M, L encoder layers of Algorithm 1, absolute position table Epos, prediction head of BERT

Ensure: the masked-token loss

  1. h0←LN(Etok[x]), with no position embedding
  2. hL−1← layers 1 to L−1 of Algorithm 1 on h0
  3. z←hL−1+Epos[1..n]
  4. for two passes do
  5. z← layer L with query from z and key and value from hL−1
  6. LMLM←∑i∈M cross-entropy of the prediction head on zi against the original xi
  7. return LMLM

Reading Algorithm 2

1–2The encoder runs with content only. Through layer L−1 the model knows distances between tokens and nothing about where in the sentence they stand.3The absolute position vectors are added once, to the output of the second-to-last layer. The paper's example is "a new store opened beside the new mall" with both nouns masked: both follow "new" at the same distance, and only the absolute place tells the subject from the object.4–5The last layer is applied twice. The query comes from the position-aware sum, the keys and values from the position-free states, and the second pass reads the first pass's output as its query. The weights of the two passes are the last layer's.6–7The head and the loss are BERT's, on the decoder's output. In fine-tuning the decoder is dropped and the encoder's own last layer is used, so a downstream model never sees absolute position.

Worked example

The topic's example script computes the row index of Algorithm 1, line 3, for a set of distances, next to the bucketed index DeBERTa V2 replaces it with. The table is shown and read in the DeBERTa V2 entry. For V1 every distance from −511 to 511 has its own row and the two outer rows gather everything beyond.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The relative table is fixed at 512 rows

With k=512 the table has 1,024 rows, and an input longer than 512 is not reachable through the position vectors either way, since every distance past 511 reads the same row. DeBERTa V2 compresses long distances onto a log scale instead.

Three scores cost three products

Each layer computes three attention matrices where BERT computes one, and the position side needs two more projections. Inference is slower than RoBERTa's at the same size, and the paper measures accuracy, not speed.

Absolute position reaches only the decoder

A downstream task that depends on where a token stands in the input, rather than on its distance to others, has to recover that from the relative pattern alone, because the fine-tuned encoder never adds the absolute vectors.

Dropping either position term costs accuracy

The paper's ablation shows every benchmark falls when the content-to-position or the position-to-content term is removed, so neither can be dropped to save compute without a loss.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/modernbert.md

ModernBERT

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of RoBERTaarXiv:2412.13663arXiv:2104.09864arXiv:2002.05202arXiv:2002.04745
In one lineRoBERTa's objective on an encoder rebuilt with rotary position, pre-norm blocks without bias, a gated GELU feed-forward, and attention that alternates every third layer between the whole text and a 128-token window, trained on two trillion tokens to a context of 8,192.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

ModernBERT keeps RoBERTa's training objective, masked language modelling without next-sentence prediction, and rebuilds the encoder with the parts decoder language models settled on between 2019 and 2024. The released base model has 22 layers of width 768 and 149M parameters, the large model 28 layers of width 1024 and 395M. Both read up to 8,192 tokens.

  • Position is rotary. Instead of a learned table, each query and key vector is rotated by an angle that grows with the token's position, so the dot product of two of them depends only on their distance. No position enters the input.
  • Attention alternates. Every third layer, starting with the first, lets every token see the whole text. The other layers let a token see 64 tokens to each side. The global layers use a rotary base of 160,000, the local layers 10,000.
  • The block is pre-norm, without bias. The layer norm sits before the attention and before the feed-forward part, not after the residual addition. Linear layers and norms have no bias term except the final decoder. The feed-forward part is a gated GELU: the input is projected to two halves, one passes through GELU and multiplies the other.
  • Training is long and staged. Two trillion tokens of English web text, code and scientific text, 30% of tokens masked, a batch warmed up to 4,608 sequences, a learning rate held constant for most of the run and decayed at the end. The first 1.7 trillion tokens run at length 1,024, then 250 billion at 8,192, then 50 billion of decay.
  • Padding is removed. Sequences in a batch are concatenated into one stream and attention is told where each begins and ends, so no compute is spent on padding tokens.

What the paper adds

The paper's claim is that encoders had stood still since RoBERTa while decoders moved, and that porting the decoder changes gives a faster and longer encoder with equal or better scores. The ablations are reported in aggregate; the paper's own comparison is against BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa V3 and the 2024 retrieval encoders on classification, retrieval and code, with a memory and speed table at lengths 512 and 8,192. It also sizes the layers so that every matrix tiles the tensor cores of common GPUs, which it calls hardware-aware design.

Why it matters here

ModernBERT is the current encoder design a small Slovenian model would copy if it copied one. Its parts are separable: rotary position, the local window, the pre-norm block and the gated feed-forward can each be taken or left, and the entry names the line of the algorithm each one sits on. The 8,192-token context matters for document-level extraction, where a relation can span paragraphs. The tokenizer is a byte-level BPE learned on English, so the tokenizer sweep's finding applies, and a Slovenian vocabulary would be the first thing to swap.
