not checked against project code. The paper says a 128-token window; the released code gives a token 64 neighbours to each side, 129 tokens in all. The first layer is global, since the code takes a layer whose index from zero is divisible by three.

Difference from predecessor

Against RoBERTa: rotary position, alternating global and local attention, pre-norm blocks without bias, a gated GELU, and a context of 8,192.

RoBERTa1, 3 to 6 and the return of BERT's Algorithm 1, against Algorithm 1 here:token, segment and absolute position embeddings summed at the input; attention over every token; a layer norm after each residual addition; a GELU feed-forward with bias
ModernBERT1, 3 to 6 and the return of BERT's Algorithm 1, against Algorithm 1 here:the token embedding alone; rotary position applied to queries and keys; attention over the whole text in every third layer and over a 64-token window either side otherwise; a layer norm before each part; a gated GELU without bias

Effect. Distance rather than place reaches every layer, two thirds of the layers cost linear time in the length, and the block trains stably at depth 22 to 28.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. ModernBERT encoder: from token ids to one vector per token

Require: token ids x1,…,xn with n≤8192, embedding table Etok, L layers of width d, window w=64, rotary bases θg=160000 and θl=10000

Ensure: hidden states hL

  1. h0←LN(Etok[x]), with no position or segment embedding and no bias in the norm
  2. for ℓ=1,…,L do
  3. g← true if (ℓ−1)mod3=0, the global layers
  4. u←hℓ−1 if ℓ=1, else LN(hℓ−1)
  5. q,k,v←Wqkvu without bias; rotate qi and ki by the angle of position i with base θg if g else θl
  6. ai←softmaxj(qi·kj/d/A)vj over all j if g, else over j with |i−j|≤w
  7. h←hℓ−1+Woa
  8. (p,z)←WinLN(h) split into two halves; hℓ←h+Wout(GELU(p)⊙z)
  9. return LN(hL)

Reading Algorithm 1

1The input is the token embedding alone, normalised once. Nothing says where a token stands; that enters through the rotation in every layer.2Layers 1, 4, 7 and so on are global, eight of the 22 in base. The rest are local.3Pre-norm: the layer norm is applied to the input of the attention, not to its output. The first layer skips it because the embedding was just normalised.4Queries, keys and values come from one projection without bias. The rotation turns each pair of coordinates of qi and ki by an angle proportional to i, with a frequency per pair set by the base. Because a rotation by i followed by one by −j is a rotation by i−j, the dot product of a rotated query and key depends on their distance only. The larger base of the global layers makes the angles grow more slowly, so distances up to 8,192 stay apart.5A global layer compares every token with every token, at quadratic cost in the length. A local layer compares a token with its 64 neighbours on each side, at linear cost. A token's view widens by 64 to each side per local layer and covers the text at every global one.6The attention output is added to the layer input. No norm follows.7The feed-forward part is gated. One projection produces two halves; GELU of the first half multiplies the second, and a projection narrows the product back. The halves are 1,152 wide in base, so the part has about as many parameters as BERT's feed-forward at inner width 3,072 would at a smaller depth.8A final norm closes the stack, which pre-norm blocks need because no norm follows the last residual addition.

Worked example

The example script lists every layer of the base model with the rule the released code applies: a layer whose index from zero is divisible by three is global, the rest are local with 64 tokens to each side.

Eight of the 22 layers see the whole text, 14 see a window of 129 tokens. At length 8,192 a local layer compares each token with 129 others where a global layer compares it with 8,192, so the local layers are about one sixtieth of the attention cost at full length.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The vocabulary is English

The 50,368-piece byte-level BPE was learned on English and code. Slovenian text is spelled in more tokens per word than with a vocabulary learned on Slovenian, which lengthens every input and spends the context on pieces.

The recipe assumes two trillion tokens

The staged schedule, the batch warmup and the constant learning rate are tuned to a run that no Slovenian corpus can fill. What the design gives at a hundredth of the data is not in the paper.

Ablations are not broken out

The paper reports the parts together and names the earlier work each came from. Which of the five changes carries the gain over RoBERTa is not separated, which is the question an experiment here would ask.

Local layers see 129 tokens

A dependency longer than 64 tokens is carried only by the eight global layers, or by stacking local layers. The paper measures retrieval and classification, not a task where one long-range link decides the answer.

Speed needs the unpadded kernels

The memory and speed figures rely on Flash Attention with variable-length sequences. Without those kernels the alternating pattern still saves compute in principle but not the measured factor.

experiments/reference/encoder-transformers/roberta.md

RoBERTa

from paperin topic Encoder Transformersvariant of BERTarXiv:1907.11692
In one lineBERT's encoder unchanged, retrained with a fresh mask on every pass, full sentences packed across document boundaries, no next-sentence prediction, a byte-level BPE vocabulary, and ten times the data at a batch of 8,000 sequences.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

RoBERTa is BERT trained differently. The layers, the widths, the absolute position table and the masking rule are all BERT's. What changes is how the training examples are made and how long and how large the training runs. The paper's point is that these choices, which BERT left under-explored, are worth as much as a new architecture.

  • The mask is drawn anew every time a sequence is seen. BERT fixed the mask when the corpus was prepared. RoBERTa draws it when the sequence is fed to the model, so every pass over the data hides different tokens.
  • Inputs are full sentences packed to 512 tokens. Sentences are taken in order from the stream of documents until the input is full. When a document ends, a separator is added and the next document continues in the same input. There is no second segment and no next-sentence label.
  • Text is cut by byte-level BPE. The vocabulary of 50,000 pieces is GPT-2's, learned over bytes, so no character is ever unknown.
  • Training is longer and wider. 160GB of text instead of 16GB, batches of 8,000 sequences instead of 256, 500,000 steps, and every step at the full length of 512 tokens.

What the paper adds

The paper is a controlled study of BERT's training recipe. It reruns BERT with one change at a time and shows which of them move the benchmarks: dynamic masking slightly, dropping next-sentence prediction slightly, larger batches and more data and longer training considerably. The byte-level vocabulary costs a little on some tasks but removes unknown tokens, which the authors take as worth it. The resulting recipe became the default for most encoders that followed.

Why it matters here

The Slovenian encoder most often used as a baseline, SloBERTa, is a RoBERTa trained with the CamemBERT recipe, so RoBERTa is the closest published design to what a Slovenian-only encoder has looked like. Its lesson for a small model is that data, batch size and training length are the first dials to set, before any change to the layers. Its byte-level vocabulary is also the byte-level BPE of this project's tokenizer sweep, so the sweep's finding on Slovenian morphology applies to this design directly.

Facts

Attention spanevery token attends to every token, as in BERT
Block normalisationpost-norm, as in BERT
ActivationGELU, as in BERT

Training dataBookCorpus and Wikipedia 16GB, CC-News 76GB, OpenWebText 38GB, Stories 31GB, in all over 160GB
OptimizerAdam with β2=0.98 and ϵ=10−6 for stability at the large batch, peak learning rate 6e-4 for Base and 4e-4 for Large, warmup over 30,000 and 24,000 steps, linear decay, weight decay 0.01
Training length500,000 steps of 8,000 sequences of 512 tokens, about two trillion tokens seen

Sources

RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach, Liu et al., 2019, arXiv:1907.11692

Difference from predecessor

Against BERT: dynamic masking, full-sentence packing, no next-sentence prediction, a byte-level BPE vocabulary, and ten times the data at a batch of 8,000.

BERT1 to 3 and the return of Algorithm 1, against lines 1 to 3 and 9 of BERT's Algorithm 2:two segments, half of them unrelated, a mask drawn once when the corpus is prepared, and the sum of the masked-token and next-sentence losses
RoBERTa1 to 3 and the return of Algorithm 1, against lines 1 to 3 and 9 of BERT's Algorithm 2:full sentences packed across documents, a mask drawn each time the sequence is fed, and the masked-token loss alone

Effect. Every pass over the data shows a different masking, every input is 512 tokens of real text, and the encoder itself is untouched.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. RoBERTa pretraining example: dynamic masking over packed full sentences

Require: a stream of documents, byte-level BPE vocabulary V of 50,000 pieces, maximum length T=512

Ensure: one input sequence and its masked-token targets

  1. take full sentences in order from the stream until T tokens are reached; when a document ends, add a separator token and continue with the next document
  2. x← <s> sentences </s>, with one segment id for every token
  3. M← 15% of the token positions of x, drawn at random now, each time x is fed to the model
  4. for all i∈M do
  5. with probability 0.8 replace xi by <mask>; with 0.1 by a random token of V; with 0.1 keep xi
  6. h← the BERT encoder (BERT, Algorithm 1) on x
  7. LMLM←∑i∈M cross-entropy of the prediction head against the original xi
  8. return LMLM

Reading Algorithm 1

1An input is filled with consecutive sentences until the length is reached, so almost every input is 512 tokens of text that belongs together. A document boundary inside the input is marked by a separator and not avoided. The paper also tried stopping at the document boundary, which scored slightly higher but gave batches of uneven size, and kept the packed form for the fixed batch size.2There is one segment, so the segment embedding carries no information. The special tokens are the start and end markers of the byte-level vocabulary.3–5The mask is drawn at the moment the sequence enters the model. Across the 500,000 steps the same sentence is hidden in a different place each time it is seen. The replacement rule inside the mask is BERT's.6–7The encoder and the prediction head are BERT's. Only the masked positions are scored.8There is no second loss. The paper found that removing next-sentence prediction matched or improved every task it measured.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The encoder is BERT's

Position is still absolute and told once, attention still spans every token, and the context is still 512. The paper changes nothing a later entry would call architecture.

A byte-level vocabulary spends pieces on bytes

The 256 byte symbols and the merges built from them are learned on English web text. A character of a language that is not English costs several bytes before it becomes a piece of its own, so a vocabulary learned on English spells Slovenian text in more tokens than a vocabulary learned on Slovenian.

The recipe is expensive

A batch of 8,000 sequences of 512 tokens for 500,000 steps is about two trillion tokens seen, over 1,000 GPUs. A small model trained on a small corpus repeats the data many times instead, and the paper does not say what happens then.

experiments/reference/information-extraction/README.md

Information Extraction

open4 entries0 checked

Which zero-shot extraction head should a small Slovenian encoder carry, and which of its parts decide what the model can return and what it can never return?

Zero-shot information extraction asks a model for entity types, labels or relations it was never trained on, named at the moment of the request. The entries here are one lineage of encoder-based extractors. Each one writes the request into the input as a prompt, runs a bidirectional encoder once over prompt and text, and matches the vectors of the request against the vectors of the text. What changes from one generation to the next is the prompt grammar, which text units are scored, how many of them, and what the decoder is allowed to return. The Compared table puts those parts side by side so an experiment can name the one it varies.

experiments/reference/information-extraction/gliner.md

GLiNER

from paperin topic Information ExtractionarXiv:2311.08526arXiv:2111.09543
In one lineEntity type names and the text go through one bidirectional encoder, every span of up to 12 words is scored against every type name by a sigmoid dot product, and the spans above 0.5 are kept greedily without overlap.
DescriptionAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

GLiNER, a generalist model for named entity recognition, finds entities of types it was never trained on. The user writes the type names, such as "person" or "organisation", and the model prepends them to the text. One bidirectional encoder reads prompt and text together, so the vector of each type name has seen the text and the vector of each word has seen the type names. The model then treats recognition as matching: every span of at most 12 words gets one vector, every type name gets one vector, and the sigmoid of their dot product says whether the span is an entity of that type. All spans and all types are scored in one pass, which is what makes it faster than a generative model that writes entities out one token at a time.

  • The prompt is part of the input. A marker token stands before each type name and a separator token closes the prompt. Both markers are new tokens whose embeddings are learned during training.
  • A span is its two ends. The span vector is built from the vector of its first word and the vector of its last word, each passed through a small feed-forward layer, then joined and projected back to the encoder width.
  • Scoring is a dot product. No head knows the type names in advance; a type is whatever its name's vector says, which is what lets the model take new types at inference.
  • Decoding is greedy. Candidates above the threshold are sorted by score and taken in order, each one skipped if it overlaps a span already taken.

What the paper adds

The paper's claim is that a 300M-parameter encoder, trained once on a corpus of 13k entity types produced by prompting a large language model, beats ChatGPT and fine-tuned generative models on zero-shot entity recognition at a fraction of the cost. It trains on Pile-NER, 44,889 passages annotated by GPT-3.5 with 240k spans, and evaluates on 20 benchmarks the model never saw, in English and in seven other languages through the multilingual DeBERTa backbone. Two regularisations matter for the claim: entity types are shuffled and some are dropped at random so the model cannot learn their order, and negative types drawn from other examples teach it to return nothing for a type the text does not contain.

Why it matters here

GLiNER is the extraction head a small Slovenian encoder would carry first, because its output is exactly what this project's task data holds. The span converter in slm4ie/data/tasks/converters/spans.py:1-14 writes every Slovenian NER dataset as GLiNER-style rows, text plus start, end and label per span, so a GLiNER head can be fine-tuned and evaluated on them without another conversion. The head is also separable from the backbone: the released multilingual model sits on mDeBERTa-v3-base, and the encoders of the encoder-transformers topic are the candidates to put under it.

Paper vs code
not checked against project code. Three differences against the released package. The paper names the markers [ENT] and [SEP]; the code uses <<ENT>> and <<SEP>>. The paper builds a span vector by one feed-forward layer over the joined end vectors; the default span mode projects each end separately, joins them, applies ReLU and projects once more. The paper trains with binary cross-entropy; the code's default is focal loss, which reduces to binary cross-entropy at its default settings, with half of the negative span and type pairs dropped from the loss at random.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. GLiNER inference: type names and text through one encoder, every span scored against every type

Require: words w1,…,wN, type names t1,…,tM, encoder E, span width K=12, threshold τ=0.5

Ensure: a set R of typed, non-overlapping spans (i,j,m)

  1. x←[ENT]t1…[ENT]tM[SEP]w1…wN
  2. H←E(x); pm← the vector at the m-th [ENT]; hi← the vector at the first subword of wi
  3. qm←FFNt(pm) for every type m
  4. for all (i,j) with 1≤i≤j≤min(i+K−1,N) do
  5. sij←FFNo(ReLU(FFNs(hi)⊕FFNe(hj)))
  6. ϕ(i,j,m)←σ(sij·qm) for every type m
  7. C←{(i,j,m):ϕ(i,j,m)>τ}, sorted by ϕ descending
  8. R←∅
  9. for all (i,j,m)∈C do
  10. if no span in R overlaps [i,j] then
  11. R←R∪{(i,j,m)}
  12. return R

Reading Algorithm 1

1The prompt is text. Each type name follows its own marker, and the separator keeps the encoder from reading the last type name into the first word. Nothing about the types is stored in the model.2One encoder pass gives every token a vector that has seen prompt and text. The type vector is read at the marker, not at the name, so a type of several words still gives one vector. A word of several subwords is read at its first subword.3A two-layer feed-forward network turns the marker vector into the type vector. The same network serves every type.4Candidate spans are every start with every width up to K, so a text of N words has about NK of them. The limit keeps the count linear in the length and discards nothing the benchmarks contain, where entities rarely exceed 12 words.5The span vector comes from its two ends. Each end is projected on its own, the two are joined, and one more projection brings the pair back to the encoder width. A span of one word uses the same vector twice.6The score is a dot product squashed to a probability. Every span and type pair is scored at once as one matrix product, which is where the parallel extraction comes from.7Only pairs above the threshold are candidates. Sorting by score decides which of two overlapping candidates wins.8** to **12Greedy decoding. A candidate is kept unless it overlaps a kept span; in the nested mode a span fully inside a kept span is also allowed. The set returned is the set of entities.

Algorithm 2. GLiNER training: one batch

Require: examples (w,G) with gold spans G⊆{(i,j,m)}, the types of the other examples in the batch, limits of 25 types per example

Ensure: updated encoder and projection weights

  1. for each example, take its gold types, add negative types drawn from the batch at a ratio of at most 1 to 1, shuffle, drop some at random, and cut to 25
  2. compute ϕ(i,j,m) for every span and type pair as Algorithm 1, lines 1 to 6
  3. y(i,j,m)←1 if (i,j,m)∈G else 0
  4. L←−∑(i,j,m)[ylogϕ+(1−y)log(1−ϕ)]
  5. return one AdamW step on L, at 10−5 for the encoder and 5·10−5 for the projections

Reading Algorithm 2

1The type list is rebuilt for every example. Negative types teach the model to return nothing for a type the text lacks. Shuffling and dropping keep it from learning a type's position.2Training scores the same span grid inference does, so there is no train-and-test gap in what is scored.3** and **4Every span and type pair is a binary decision. Gold spans are positives; all other pairs, including gold spans under the wrong type, are negatives.5The encoder moves slowly and the fresh projections faster. The paper runs 30,000 such steps with a cosine schedule.

Worked example

The example script lays out the prompt the released multilingual model builds for one Slovenian sentence with two type names, and counts the spans it scores at several text lengths.

A text of 32 words gives 318 spans per type. At 512 words the grid is 6,078 spans per type, still linear in the length because the width is capped, but each span is scored against every type, so a prompt of 20 types at 512 words scores over 120,000 pairs.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Twelve words is a hard ceiling

A span of 13 or more words cannot be returned, whatever the score. Titles of works, addresses and legal citations in Slovenian text exceed it.

The prompt eats the context

Type names and the text share 384 subword tokens. Twenty Slovenian type names spelled by an English-trained tokenizer take a large share of it before the text begins.

Spans only

One span, one type. A relation between two spans, a label for the whole text, or an attribute of a span has no place in the output.

Silver training data

Pile-NER was annotated by GPT-3.5 with no human check, and its types are whatever the annotator named. What the model learned as "person" is that annotator's notion of a person.

experiments/reference/information-extraction/gliner2-5.md

GLiNER2.5

from paperin topic Information Extractionvariant of GLiNER2arXiv:2507.18546
In one lineGLiNER2's schema prompt on a boundary head that scores where spans start and end instead of enumerating a span grid, pairs the best boundaries sparsely so a span may have any length, adds typed relations and span attributes, and hands every score to a constrained decoder on a 4,096-word context.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

GLiNER2.5 keeps GLiNER2's prompt and encoder and replaces the span grid. For each request, called a query, the model scores every token boundary as a possible start, every token boundary as a possible end, and every token as being inside a span of that query. A proposal stage keeps the best starts and, for each, the best ends that follow it, then the same backwards from the best ends, and the union, cut to a budget, is the candidate set. Each candidate pair is then rescored with the inside evidence between its ends and its length. Because a start may pair with any later end, a span can open at the first token and close at the last, and the work stays linear in the text length for a fixed schema and budget.

  • Relations are typed pairs of mentions. A relation group names a head role and a tail role, and the schema says which entity types may fill each. For every relation type the best head-typed and tail-typed mentions are paired and scored together with the relation's query vector.
  • Attributes classify a span. An attribute such as sentiment or negation is a classification whose query is scored on an already extracted span, so a mention carries its own labels.
  • Records lose the count head. A record is formed around an anchor field; every anchor candidate seeds one record and the other fields are assigned to a record or declared absent.
  • Decoding is constrained. Classification tasks may declare rules between labels, relations declare their endpoint types and multiplicity, and the decoder returns only assignments that satisfy them; the type-safe-encoder entry describes it.

What the paper adds

There is no paper. The release note states three claims: a span may have any length within the window, inference stays linear in the length, and outputs satisfy the declared schema. On the vendor's zero-shot suite the multilingual model scores level with GLiNER2 overall and far above it on natural language inference, and its training data was generated by the vendor's own data agent rather than drawn from public corpora.

Why it matters here

GLiNER2.5 is the current shape of the head this project would train, and the first whose candidate count does not grow with a width limit: a Slovenian document of 4,000 words is scored on 192 candidates per query instead of a grid of tens of thousands. Its relation and attribute heads cover what the NER benchmarks here do not. The cost is that none of its parts has a paper and the recipe exists only as code, so what a Slovenian backbone would need of it is read from the implementation.

Difference from predecessor

Against GLiNER2: a sparse boundary proposal replaces the width-limited span grid; relations, attributes and constrained decoding are added.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. GLiNER2.5 inference: boundary scores, sparse pairing and rescoring, one query

Require: words w1,…,wN, a schema prompt as GLiNER2 with [R] roles, encoder E, budgets k0=24, α=0.08, kmax=128, ends per start e=12, candidate budget C=192, threshold τ=0.5

Ensure: scored spans per query, handed to the constrained decoder

  1. H←E(x) with x as GLiNER2's Algorithm 1, line 1; u← the vector at the query's field marker; hi← the vector at the first subword of wi
  2. bi←LN(Wo[Wlhi⊕Wrhi+1]) for the N+1 boundaries, with learned vectors before w1 and after wN; two attention blocks over a window of 128 boundaries and one gated feed-forward block refine b
  3. ai←⟨Wsbi,Ws′u⟩/d, ei←⟨Webi,We′u⟩/d, ni←⟨Wnhi,Wn′u⟩/d: start, end and inside scores
  4. k←min(kmax,⌈max(k0,⌈αN⌉)/8⌉·8); S← the k boundaries with the largest ai; T← the k with the largest ei
  5. P←{(i,j):i∈S,j among the e ends after i with the largest ⟨g(u)⊙Wpbi,Wqbj⟩+ej}∪{(i,j):j∈T,i among the e starts before j likewise}
  6. Cq← the C pairs of P with the largest proposal score, duplicates removed
  7. for all (i,j)∈Cq do
  8. ℓij←compat(bi,bj,u)+ai+ej+priorij+ω(u)·∑i≤t<jnt/j−i+λ(u)·len(i,j)+content(i,j,u)
  9. Rq←{(i,j):σ(ℓij)≥τ}, extended to the count head's predicted number when adaptive, overlaps resolved by score
  10. relations: for each relation type, the 32 best head-typed and 32 best tail-typed mentions of R, at most 64 pairs, scored by a bilinear layer over the two mention vectors and the relation's query
  11. labels: σ(MLPl(ug,k)) per label marker; attributes: the attribute query scored on each extracted span of the types it applies to
  12. return every candidate with its score, for the constrained decoder

Reading Algorithm 1

1The prompt and encoder are GLiNER2's. Each field marker, including the head and tail roles of a relation, is one query with its own vector.2A boundary sits between two words. Its vector joins the word on its left and the word on its right, so the start of a span is described by what precedes it and what it begins with. Learned vectors stand in for the missing neighbour at the two ends of the text. Local attention lets boundaries see 128 neighbours and a feed-forward block refines them.3Three scores per query, each a scaled dot product with the query vector: how much a boundary looks like a start, how much like an end, and how much a token looks like part of the span. The inside scores are summed into a running total so any interval's inside evidence is one subtraction.4The budget grows with the length, from 24 boundaries to at most 128, rounded up to a multiple of 8 so batches share shapes. The top starts and the top ends are chosen by their scores alone.5Each chosen start is paired with the 12 ends after it that fit it best, by a gated dot product between the two boundary vectors plus the end score; each chosen end is paired with the 12 starts before it likewise. No term depends on the distance, which is what removes the width limit. At most 2·k·e pairs are ever materialised.6The two directions are merged, duplicates collapsed, and the 192 best pairs kept. This is the candidate set; nothing outside it can be returned.7** and **8Each candidate is rescored with everything known about it: the endpoint compatibility through 8 heads, its start and end scores, the proposal score as a prior, the mean inside score of the tokens between its ends, three length features, and a pooled vector of its content. The query decides how much the inside and length terms weigh.9A candidate is an entity if its sigmoid clears the threshold. With adaptive decoding, a count head's Poisson rate fills the list up to the predicted number. The flat policy drops a candidate that overlaps a better one.10Relations reuse the extracted mentions. The schema says which types may be a head and which a tail, so only typed pairs are formed, and a cap keeps the pair count fixed. A bilinear scorer reads both mention vectors and the relation's query.11Labels are classified from their markers as in GLiNER2. An attribute is a classification run on a span: the attribute's query is scored on each extracted span of the types it applies to.12Nothing is final here. Candidates, relations and labels go to the constrained decoder, which decides what the schema allows.

Worked example

The candidate-counts table compares the span grids of the two predecessors with the boundary budget at several lengths, computed with the released configuration's rule.

Up to 128 words the budget stays at 24 starts and 24 ends; at 512 it is 48 and from about 1,600 words it is capped at 128. The pairs proposed grow from 576 to 3,072, and the candidates actually rescored never exceed 192 per query, where GLiNER2's grid at 4,096 words holds 32,740 spans per type.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

No paper

The method, its losses and its training data are described in a release note and a model card. The claims are the vendor's own benchmarks. An experiment here would be the first independent measurement.

A span outside the budget is lost

If a gold span's start is not among the k best starts, or its end not among the 12 best ends for that start or the reverse, it is never scored. Recall on long or unusual spans depends on the proposer, and the proposer is trained with gold pairs injected, which inference lacks.

The budget is per query, the pool per text

The shared candidate pool is built once from the start and end scores of all queries, so a query with few strong boundaries competes with the others for the same 192 slots.

Thresholds and budgets are tuned to the vendor's data

Every number above, from the window of 128 to the 20 hard negatives, is a configuration value chosen on undisclosed training data. Which of them a Slovenian retraining must keep is unknown.

experiments/reference/information-extraction/gliner2.md

GLiNER2

from paperin topic Information Extractionvariant of GLiNERarXiv:2507.18546
In one lineGLiNER's span matching behind a schema prompt that composes entity types, classification labels and record fields in one input, with a count head for how many records to fill and a label head for classification, on a 2,048-token context.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

GLiNER2 keeps GLiNER's idea, one encoder over prompt and text and a dot product between request vectors and span vectors, and widens what a request may be. The request is a schema: a list of entity types, a classification task with its labels, or a record type with named fields, and several of these at once. Each part of the schema becomes a bracketed group in the prompt with its own marker tokens, the groups are joined by a separator, and the text follows. One forward pass then serves every group.

  • Entities work as in GLiNER. Each type marker's vector is matched against every span of at most 8 words.
  • Records are entities with a count. A record type such as "employment" has fields such as "employee" and "employer". A small head reads the group's prompt marker and predicts how many records the text holds, from 0 to 19. For each record, a recurrent layer stamps the field vectors with the record's index, and each stamped field vector is matched against the spans as an entity type would be. The result is a list of filled records rather than a flat list of spans.
  • Classification reads the label markers. Each label's marker vector goes through a small classifier that outputs one logit. A single-label task takes the largest; a multi-label task keeps every label above 0.5.
  • Descriptions and examples ride in the prompt. A type or label may carry a short description and a task may carry a few labelled examples, written after the group's name behind their own marker tokens.

What the paper adds

The paper's claim is that one encoder under 500M parameters can replace a large language model for entity recognition, text classification and structured extraction at once, on a CPU. It trains a 205M-parameter model on 254,334 examples, 135,698 from news, Wikipedia, legal text, arXiv and PubMed annotated by GPT-4o and 118,636 synthetic ones from emails, messages, resumes and e-commerce text, and reports results against GLiNER and against prompted large models on zero-shot NER, classification and record extraction. The released package adds a schema builder and LoRA fine-tuning.

Why it matters here

GLiNER2 is the first entry whose output covers more than entity spans, which is what a Slovenian extraction benchmark beyond NER would need: sentiment and the SuperGLUE-SL tasks this project prepares are classification, and a record schema fits event-like annotations. Its parts are separable from the backbone in the same way GLiNER's are, so a Slovenian encoder can take the span head, the count head and the label head as they stand. The multilingual release again sits on mDeBERTa-v3-base.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. GLiNER2 inference: one forward pass over a composed schema

Require: words w1,…,wN, schema groups g1,…,gG each with a name and fields fg,1,…,fg,k, encoder E, span width K=8

Ensure: entities per type, filled records per record type, labels per classification task

  1. x←group(g1)[SEP_STRUCT]…group(gG)[SEP_TEXT]w1…wN, with group(g)=([P] name (μ fg,1…μ fg,k)) and μ one of [E], [C], [L]
  2. H←E(x); pg← the vector at the [P] of group g; ug,k← the vector at its k-th field marker; hi← the vector at the first subword of wi
  3. for all entity groups g do
  4. score every span (i,j) with j−i<K against every ug,k as GLiNER's Algorithm 1, lines 4 to 12
  5. for all record groups g do
  6. n←\argmaxc∈0..19MLPc(pg)
  7. ug,k(r)←T(GRU(er,ug,k)+ug,k) for r=1..n, with er a learned embedding of the record index and T a small transformer
  8. record r, field k← the span with the highest σ(sij·ug,k(r)), or every span above 0.5 for a list field
  9. for all classification groups g do
  10. zg,k←MLPl(ug,k); single-label: the k with the largest z; multi-label: every k with σ(zg,k)>0.5
  11. return the entities, records and labels

The group's name follows the prompt marker, its fields follow their own marker, and the marker's kind says what the fields are: entity types, record fields or labels. Several groups sit in one prompt, which is what lets one pass serve several tasks.2As in GLiNER, vectors are read at the markers. Each group gives one prompt vector and one vector per field.3** and **4Entity groups are plain GLiNER with a shorter width. Every span of at most 8 words is scored against every type vector and decoded greedily.5** and **6A record group first decides how many records the text holds. The classifier over the prompt vector has 20 outputs, 0 to 19, and the largest wins.7Each record needs its own field vectors, or every record would fill the same spans. A learned embedding of the record index is fed with the field vector through a GRU, the field vector is added back, and a two-layer transformer lets the fields of one record see each other.8A stamped field vector is matched against the spans exactly as a type vector is. The best span fills the field; a field declared as a list takes every span above threshold.9** and **10Classification never looks at spans. Each label's marker vector goes through a classifier that outputs one logit. Worked example

The prompt-layouts table shows the input the released processor builds for the toy sentence with an entity group, a classification group, a record group and all of them composed, and the candidate-counts table shows how many spans the width of 8 yields.

The shorter width cuts the grid by about a third against GLiNER at every length, from 318 to 228 spans per type at 32 words.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Eight words is a harder ceiling than twelve

A span of nine or more words cannot be returned. Slovenian organisation names and titles exceed it more often than English ones.

Nineteen records at most

The count head has 20 outputs. A text with more records than that fills nineteen and drops the rest.

No relations

Two spans can share a record but the model never scores a pair of spans as such. A relation type with head and tail roles arrives only in GLiNER2.5.

Tasks do not see each other's answers

Each group is decoded on its own. A label combination the schema forbids, such as a harm type under a "safe" verdict, can be returned, which is what the type-safe decoding of the successor exists to prevent.

experiments/reference/information-extraction/type-safe-encoder.md

Type-safe encoder models

from paperin topic Information Extractionpart of GLiNER2.5arXiv:2609.26758
In one lineThe decoders behind GLiNER2.5 that take every score of the encoder and return only an assignment the declared schema allows, an exact search with pruning for label rules and a beam search over typed entity and relation candidates, so a returned output is well-typed by construction.
DescriptionAlgorithmWorked exampleWhere it sitsEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

A type-safe encoder model is an extractor whose output is guaranteed to fit the schema the user declared, not merely likely to. The encoder itself does not change: GLiNER2.5 scores every label, span and relation independently, as its predecessors did. What changes is that the scores are not thresholded one by one. The schema is compiled into a set of constraints, and a decoder searches for the assignment with the highest total score among those that satisfy every constraint. If no assignment satisfies them, the decoder says so instead of returning something invalid.

Two decoders exist, one per kind of output.

  • Constrained classification. A classification schema declares tasks, each single-label, multi-label or ordinal, and rules between them written as logic: a label implies another, two labels exclude each other, a task selects at least or at most so many labels, an ordinal task sits at or above a level. Every rule is a three-valued expression, true, false or not yet decided, so a partial assignment can be pruned as soon as a rule is false. The decoder enumerates each task's feasible label sets, orders tasks by how many rules touch them, and runs a depth-first search with a bound that skips any branch that cannot beat the best complete assignment.
  • Joint entity and relation extraction. A joint schema declares entity types, relation types with the entity types allowed as head and tail, and rules such as at most one relation per head, no self loops, no cycles, or that a relation is symmetric. Entity and relation candidates become nodes and edges with scores. A beam search adds edges in score order, each time keeping both the state with and the state without the edge, admitting an edge only if its endpoints exist, their types are allowed and every rule still holds. The best feasible finished state is returned.

"Type-safe" names the guarantee: a relation's head is always an entity of a declared head type, a label combination the rules forbid is never returned, and a field declared as a choice holds one of its choices. It does not name accuracy. A well-typed output can still be wrong.

Why it matters here

An extraction benchmark here will be scored by exact match of structured output, and an invalid structure, such as a relation whose head is not an entity, is a miss that no amount of model quality fixes. The constrained decoders are pure Python with no dependence on the encoder, so they can sit on any head this project trains, including a GLiNER head on a Slovenian backbone, and the gain they give can be measured on its own by decoding the same scores with and without the rules.

Paper vs code
no paper. Against the release note, the code adds a rescue rule: a label a constraint names is kept as a candidate even below the retention floor, so a rule can force a low-scoring label, and an entity span a relation needs is rescued into the node set even when its own score fell below the entity threshold. Algorithm

Algorithm 1. Constrained classification: exact search over feasible label sets

Require: tasks t1,…,tT with labels and cardinality bounds, rules 𝒞, logits zt,l, retention floor 0.5, cap 64

Ensure: the feasible assignment with the highest utility, or none

  1. compile: every rule names declared tasks and labels; the rules are satisfiable on the declared label sets; a task with a default label gets the rule that the default holds iff no other label does
  2. for all tasks t do
  3. ut,l←zt,l−logit(τt); keep labels with σ(zt,l)≥0.5, at most 64, plus every label a rule names
  4. Lt← the feasible label sets of t: one per label for a single-label task, every subset within the bounds when a rule reads the whole selection, else subsets of the rule-named labels completed with the positive free labels; each with utility ∑u, sorted descending
  5. order tasks by the number of rules touching them, descending; boundi←∑k≥imaxLtk; u⋆←−∞
  6. for all sets l∈Lti in order, at depth i of the search do
  7. if u+ul+boundi+1≤u⋆ then
  8. stop this task: every later set scores lower
  9. if every rule touching ti is true or undecided under the partial assignment then
  10. descend to ti+1 with u+ul; at the last task set u⋆←u+ul and record the assignment
  11. return the recorded assignment, or none when no branch reached the last task

Reading Algorithm 1

1Compilation rejects a schema that can never be satisfied, before any text is scored. A default label becomes an ordinary rule so the search needs no special case for it.2** and **3A label's utility is its logit minus the threshold's logit, so the sum of utilities is the log-odds of the whole assignment against the thresholds. Labels below the floor are dropped, except those a rule names: a rule may force a label the model scored low, and dropping it would make the schema infeasible for a reason the model never saw.4Rather than search over labels, the search runs over each task's feasible label sets. For a single-label task that is one set per label. For a multi-label task the free labels, which no rule mentions, are always taken when positive, so only the rule-named labels are enumerated.5Tasks with many rules go first because their choice prunes the most. The bound at each depth is what the remaining tasks could add at best.6** to **8Sets are visited in utility order, so the first set that cannot beat the best complete assignment ends the task's loop: every later set is worse.9** and **10A rule is evaluated in three values. False prunes the branch; undecided, because a task the rule reads is not yet assigned, lets the search go on. At the last task the assignment is complete and feasible.11None means no feasible assignment exists among the retained labels. The caller then raises an infeasibility error, or in relaxed mode widens retention to every label and, failing that, returns the assignment with the fewest violations.

Algorithm 2. Joint entity and relation decoding: beam search over typed candidates

Require: entity candidates V with type, span and utility; relation candidates A with head, tail, slot and utility; compiled rules 𝒞; beam width 32

Ensure: the feasible set of entities and relations with the highest score

  1. compile: each relation gets typed endpoints, no self loops, a unique pair, a unique slot, and its declared per-head and per-tail limits; entities get the overlap policy
  2. V← spans with probability ≥0.05, at most 32 per type; A← pairs of the 12 best head and tail role spans per slot, joined to nodes of the allowed types, rescued into V if missing, at most 128 per slot
  3. order A by edge utility plus both endpoint utilities, descending; B←{∅}
  4. for all edges a∈A in order do
  5. for all states s∈B do
  6. keep s unchanged, the skip
  7. if a's slot is free in s, its new endpoints pass the overlap policy, every rule allows a after s's edges, and the gain ua+∑unew nodes≥0 then
  8. add s∪{a} with score + gain
  9. merge states with equal nodes, edges and slots; keep the 32 best
  10. finish every state with each positive node the rules allow; add the greedy solution as one more candidate
  11. drop every candidate that fails a full re-check, including symmetric and inverse completeness
  12. return the surviving candidate with the highest score, else the empty set marked infeasible

Reading Algorithm 2

1The schema is lowered to rule objects. Typed endpoints come from the relation's declared head and tail types; the per-slot rule keeps each relation instance to one pair.2Candidates are capped so the search is bounded. A span the relation scorer wants as an endpoint but the entity scorer dropped is rescued, because a relation cannot exist without its nodes.3Edges are ranked by what taking them is worth, endpoints included, so a strong relation can bring in a weak entity.4** to **8Each edge is offered to every state in the beam, and each state spawns a copy without it and, if allowed, a copy with it. The checks are the schema's rules, evaluated against the edges already in the state, so a second relation on a head limited to one is refused.9Equal states are merged and the beam cut, which keeps the search linear in the number of edges.10Entities need no relation to be returned, so every finished state is topped up with the positive nodes the rules admit. The greedy solution is added as a candidate so the beam never does worse than greedy.11Symmetric and inverse rules are whole-result properties and cannot be checked edge by edge; every candidate is re-validated in full.12The best feasible candidate wins. When none is feasible the empty set is returned with an infeasibility flag, which is the guarantee: never an invalid structure.

Worked example

The example script runs the released solver and beam search on toy scores.

The classification schema has a single-label task "safety" with labels safe and unsafe, a multi-label task "harm" with labels violence and fraud, and one rule: any selected harm implies unsafe. The logits make the text read as safe on its own while violence scores high.

Independent decoding returns safe with violence, which the rule forbids. The constrained decoder returns unsafe with violence: the rule leaves two feasible assignments, safe alone or unsafe with violence, and the second has the higher utility. The utility falls from 3.5 to 2.1, which is the price of feasibility.

The joint schema has types person and organisation and a relation works_for from a person to an organisation, limited to one per head and one per tail. The toy sentence "Ana Novak vodi Krko, Lek pa vodi Maja Kos." gives four entity candidates, one spurious organisation "Novak" inside the person span, and four relation candidates, one of them from an organisation to an organisation.

Greedy takes the strongest relation first, Ana Novak to Lek, which then blocks both Ana Novak to Krko by the per-head limit and Maja Kos to Lek by the per-tail limit, for a total of 2.0. The beam keeps the state that skipped that edge and ends with the two weaker relations, for 2.8. Both decoders drop the organisation-to-organisation edge by its endpoint types and the nested "Novak" by the overlap policy.

Where it sits

The decoders are the last stage of GLiNER2.5. The encoder and its heads produce logits for every label, span and relation candidate; the candidate builder turns them into utilities and caps them; the decoder picks the assignment; a result builder maps spans back to character offsets. The same decoders serve GLiNER2.5-Decide, the vendor's decision model, where each question is a classification task and the rules connect answers.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

Well-typed is not correct

The guarantee covers the structure of the output and nothing about its content. The 2026 study of typed decision models finds that renaming the options of a question flips up to 70 points of decisions while the type-error rate stays at zero: the models follow the option's name, not its definition.

The rules are the user's

Nothing is learned about which combinations are valid. A rule left out is not enforced, and a rule written wrong makes the schema infeasible or forces a wrong label with full confidence.

Infeasibility is a hard stop

When the rules admit no assignment over the retained candidates, the default is an error, not a best effort. The relaxed mode returns the assignment with the fewest violations, which is then not well-typed.

The search is bounded

Exact search stops at 200,000 nodes and falls back to a beam; the joint beam holds 32 states. A schema with many interacting rules or many relation slots may return a feasible but not optimal assignment.

Related

Part ofGLiNER2.5GLiNER2's schema prompt on a boundary head that scores where spans start and end instead of enumerating a span grid, pairs the best boundaries sparsely so a span may have any length, adds typed relations and span attributes, and hands every score to a constrained decoder on a 4,096-word context.

experiments/reference/subword-tokenizers/README.md

Subword tokenizers

open8 entries6 checked

How should Slovenian words be cut into tokens, and at which step can a morpheme boundary be enforced?

A subword tokenizer cuts text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary, so that a rare word is spelled from pieces the model has seen. A morpheme is the smallest part of a word that carries meaning, such as a stem or an ending. The entries here learn their vocabulary from the same corpus sample. They differ in what they start from, how they pick the next token, and how they cut a new word.

#23Drop intermediate BPE tokens during training, as Picky-BPE and Scaffold-BPE do

Training, the merge loop#23open

BPE keeps every token it ever formed, including those that exist only as stepping stones to longer tokens. On their own they are rare, their embeddings stay under-trained, and they hold slots that could go to whole stems and endings. Picky-BPE (Chizhov et al., EMNLP 2024, https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.925/) removes a part whose uses are almost all inside the new merge, measured as the pair count over the part's own count against a threshold. Scaffold-BPE (Lian et al., arXiv:2404.17808) removes a part whose remaining count falls below the count of the merge just made. Both report no loss in compression and equal or better downstream scores.

#24Protect only the stem during BPE training, as the Slovak morphological tokenizer does

Training, how a word is chunked before pairs are counted#24open

MorphBPE forbids every merge across a lexicon boundary, so an ending never joins its stem and the vocabulary may not fill. The Slovak morphological tokenizer SKMT (Držík and Forgáč, PeerJ Computer Science 2024, doi:10.7717/peerj-cs.2465, with a follow-up in Expert Systems with Applications 312, 2026) protects only the root: it is one atomic symbol from the start, and the letters around it merge freely, including onto the root. A small Slovak masked model trained with it reached lower perplexity than BPE and gained on semantic similarity and question answering.

experiments/reference/subword-tokenizers/bpe-knockout.md

BPE-knockout

from paperin topic Subword tokenizersvariant of Byte-level BPEdoi:10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-long.324
In one lineByte-level BPE whose finished merge list is pruned afterwards; every merge that more often than not glues two morphemes together is removed, and the merges built on it take its parts instead.
DescriptionDifferenceDefinitionAlgorithmEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) learns its merges from counts alone, so many merges glue the end of one morpheme to the start of the next, where a morpheme is the smallest meaning-bearing part of a word. BPE-knockout takes a finished BPE tokenizer and a reference list of words already cut at their morpheme boundaries. It runs the tokenizer over every reference word and blames the merge that deleted each boundary the reference keeps. A merge that is blamed in at least half of its uses is knocked out. Its token leaves the vocabulary, but every later merge that consumed that token now consumes the token's parts, so the rest of the tokenizer keeps working. The result is a byte-tuple tokenizer: a merge may join more than two pieces at once.

  • Nothing is retrained. The method edits an existing tokenizer and keeps most of its merges. The paper applied it to the tokenizer of a trained Dutch language model and continued that model's pretraining.
  • The lexicon is read once, after training. Encoding replays the pruned merges and consults no lexicon.
  • The vocabulary shrinks. Each knocked-out merge frees one slot. In the paper about a tenth of a 40,000-token vocabulary went.

What the paper adds

The paper writes BPE as a graph of merges with two invariants, every merge has two parents and every token is made by exactly one merge, and shows that the second invariant is what lets a token be removed without breaking the merges above it. It defines the blame ratio and reports the gains below on the CELEX lexicons of English, Dutch and German, with word tokens weighted by their frequency in the OSCAR web corpus. Those are the paper's results, not this project's.

Change against plain BPE, 40,000 tokens Word types Word tokens
Morpheme-boundary precision about +10 +5 to +45
Morpheme-boundary recall about +25 +50 to +60
Morpheme-boundary F1 about +15 +50 to +60
Compound-boundary recall about +10 +50 to +70

Two Dutch RoBERTa models were pretrained from scratch, one per tokenizer. The plain BPE model kept a lower pseudo-perplexity and won most fine-tuning tasks except named-entity recognition. Switching the plain BPE model's tokenizer to the pruned one and pretraining for 5,000 more batches then beat both on the token-level tasks, with part-of-speech accuracy rising from 93.8 to 96.0 and named-entity F1 from 84.0 to 87.5, while sequence-level tasks stayed level. Random dropout of merges, the usual regulariser, lowered precision instead.

Why it matters here

Byte-level BPE is the baseline of the tokenizer sweep, and this method edits it after training with no new training run. It enforces a morpheme boundary at a third step: MorphBPE does so while training, MorphPiece while encoding, and BPE-knockout once training is over. The Sloleks-derived lexicon the sweep already holds is a flat list of forms cut into stem and ending, which is the only input the blame step needs.

The paper's adaptation result also matters on its own. A Slovenian model that already exists could keep its weights and get a tokenizer that follows morphology, at the cost of a short continued pretraining.

Facts

Picks next token byhighest pair count, followed by a pruning pass that removes every merge whose blame ratio is at least one half
Encodingthe pruned merges replayed in their original priority, a merge joining all its parts at once; no lexicon
Needs lexicononce, after training, a word list cut at morpheme boundaries
Settingthe blame threshold, one half in the paper; whether blame counts each reference word once or weights it by frequency, once in the paper
Vocabularythe predecessor's size less the knocked-out tokens, about 9 to 11% fewer in the paper

Repeatableyes; the order in which merges are knocked out does not change the result

Sources

Paper
BPE-knockout: Pruning Pre-existing BPE Tokenisers with Backwards-compatible Morphological Semi-supervision, Bauwens and Delobelle, NAACL 2024, doi:10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-long.324

Difference from predecessor

Against Byte-level BPE: a pruning pass guided by a morpheme lexicon follows training.

Byte-level BPEafter line 11 of the training algorithm:return a standard BPE model holding S, V and M
BPE-knockoutafter line 11 of the training algorithm:blame every merge on the reference lexicon, knock out each merge with R(m)≥1/2, return the pruned tuple merges

Effect. Merges that glue morphemes together disappear, the merges above them take their parts, and the cuts fall on morpheme boundaries more often.

Definition

For a merge m, let N(m) be how many times it was applied while encoding the reference words and B(m) how many of those applications deleted a boundary the reference keeps. The blame ratio is

R(m)=B(m)N(m)

and a merge is knocked out when R(m)≥1/2. The threshold is a heuristic the paper keeps fixed.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. Blame: choosing the merges to knock out

Require: trained merges M in priority order, reference words W each cut at its morpheme boundaries

Ensure: the set K of merges to remove

  1. N(m)←0 and B(m)←0 for every merge m
  2. for all words w in W do
  3. encode w by replaying M, and note for every deleted space which merge deleted it
  4. for all merges m applied in w do
  5. N(m)←N(m)+1
  6. if m deleted a space that the reference cut of w keeps then
  7. B(m)←B(m)+1
  8. return K←{m:B(m)/N(m)≥1/2}

Reading Algorithm 1

1Every merge starts with a clean record.2–3The tokenizer runs as usual over each reference word. Each space deleted between two characters was deleted by exactly one merge, so blame has one owner.4–7A merge is counted every time it fires, and blamed when it fired across a boundary. It is enough that the merge glued one character of each morpheme; once a boundary is gone no later merge can restore it.8The ratio compares harm to use. Each word counts once, so rare words weigh as much as common ones.

Algorithm 2. Knockout: removing one token from the merge graph

Require: vocabulary V, for every token its forming merge Mi(t) and the merges Mo(t) that consume it, the token t to remove

Ensure: the graph without t

  1. if t has no forming merge then
  2. return the graph unchanged, t is a byte symbol
  3. mold← the one merge in Mi(t), with parts p1,…,pn
  4. for all parts pi do
  5. remove mold from Mo(pi)
  6. for all merges q in Mo(t) do
  7. replace t among the parts of q by p1,…,pn, keeping the priority of q
  8. for all parts pi do
  9. add q to Mo(pi)
  10. remove t from V, and empty Mi(t) and Mo(t)
  11. return the graph

Reading Algorithm 2

1–2A byte symbol was never merged into being, so it cannot be knocked out.3–5The merge that made t is cut loose from its parents.6–9Every merge that needed t now needs the parts of t instead, at the same priority. This is the step that stops the removal from cascading: a merge above t keeps working, only with more parts.10–11The token is gone. Its parts and its consumers stay.

Algorithm 3. Byte-tuple encoding

Require: word w as byte symbols, pruned merges M′ in priority order

Ensure: the tokens of w

  1. while some merge in M′ matches adjacent symbols of w do
  2. apply the matching merge of highest priority, joining all of its parts into one symbol
  3. return the symbols of w

Reading Algorithm 3

1–2Encoding is the predecessor's with one change: a merge may have more than two parts and joins them in one step. Priorities are the original ones, so a word with no knocked-out merge is cut exactly as before.3What is left when no merge applies is the token sequence.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

The reference sets the ceiling

Blame finds only the boundaries the reference knows. The Sloleks-derived cuts of this project mark the boundary between stem and ending, so a merge across a prefix, a suffix that builds a new word, or a compound seam goes unblamed unless the derivational source is configured.

Recall rises, whole-word precision falls

More boundaries are kept, so more cuts land inside what the reference treats as one word. The paper reports drops in compound-boundary precision of up to 10 points on frequency-weighted tokens, and the morpheme-boundary F1 still rises.

Gains from scratch were not uniform

The Dutch model pretrained from scratch with the pruned tokenizer lost to plain BPE on perplexity and on most fine-tuning tasks. The clear gains came from adapting an existing model, and the paper offers only a speculative reason.

The tokenizer leaves the standard format

A merge with three or more parts cannot be stored in a HuggingFace BPE model, so the pruned tokenizer needs the authors' package or a custom encoder at training and inference time.

The threshold is a guess

One half was chosen as a plain heuristic. A different threshold prunes more or less, and the paper's appendix explores it without fixing a better value.

Related

PredecessorByte-level BPECharacter BPE run over the bytes of the text instead of its characters, with the space before a word kept as part of the word.

experiments/reference/subword-tokenizers/byte-level-bpe.md

Byte-level BPE

checked against codein topic Subword tokenizersvariant of Character BPEarXiv:1909.03341
In one lineCharacter BPE run over the bytes of the text instead of its characters, with the space before a word kept as part of the word.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) builds a vocabulary of word pieces by joining the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols, again and again, until the vocabulary is full. Byte-level BPE runs the same procedure over the UTF-8 bytes of the text rather than over its characters. Every byte is shown as one printable character, so the pieces are still strings, and the 256 byte symbols are the starting vocabulary. A new word is cut by replaying the merges in the order they were learned.

  • Nothing is ever unknown. Every character is a sequence of bytes, and all 256 byte symbols are in the vocabulary, so any text can be spelled.
  • A space belongs to the word after it. Text is cut into words, numbers and runs of punctuation, and each keeps the space in front of it, shown as Ġ. A piece therefore knows whether it begins a word, and decoding returns the exact text, spaces included.
  • A Slovenian letter outside ASCII is two symbols. š, č and ž are two bytes each, shown as Å¡, Äį and Å¾, so a merge is spent on rebuilding each before a stem can form.

What the paper adds

The GPT-2 report introduced this scheme to get the open vocabulary of bytes without the long byte sequences that plain byte BPE produces. Its one rule is to stop merges from crossing between letters, digits and punctuation, with the space before a word as the only exception. The report's language-model results are not this project's.

Why it matters here

Byte-level BPE is the usual tokenizer of language-model pretraining, used by GPT-2, RoBERTa and ModernBERT, and it is the fallback path of MorphPiece in this project's sweep. Its scores set the bar that every morpheme-aware tokenizer has to beat. It differs from MorphBPE in its base unit as well as in the boundary rule, so the pair that isolates the rule is Character BPE against MorphBPE, not this entry.

Facts

Base unitUTF-8 bytes, each shown as one printable character
Chunk while trainingwhole word, with the space before it
Picks next token byhighest pair count, a tie going to the pair whose symbols entered the vocabulary first
Encodingstandard BPE merges, no lexicon
Needs lexiconno
Settingvocabulary size, which includes the special tokens and the 256 byte symbols
Unknown tokennone, every character is spelled from its bytes
Round tripdecoding returns the exact text, spaces included
Repeatableyes, training has no random step
Exporta standard tokenizer.json, loaded as a fast tokenizer
Registry keybpe

Sources

Paper
Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners, Radford et al., OpenAI, 2019, section 2.2
Neural Machine Translation with Byte-Level Subwords, arXiv:1909.03341, which names the method and studies it on its own
Code
slm4ie/tokenizers/backends/hf_bpe.py
slm4ie/tokenizers/backends/_hf_base.py
Example
experiments/reference/subword-tokenizers/examples.py
Paper vs code
The report cuts text with one pattern that keeps letters, digits and punctuation apart and attaches the space before a word to it. The code uses the same pattern through the byte-level pre-tokenizer of the HuggingFace tokenizers library.
The report puts no space before the first word of a text, so that word is a different symbol from the same word inside a text. The code adds the space, so every word at the start of a line is spelled like one inside it.
The report has one special token. The code adds the sweep's five and counts them toward the vocabulary size.
The report does not say how a tie between equally frequent pairs is broken. The code takes the pair whose symbols entered the vocabulary first. The example script checks this on five ties.
The merge loop itself runs inside the HuggingFace tokenizers library. The code sets its inputs and reads its output, so the loop lines cite no project code, and the example script checks each learned merge against a replay of the pair counts.
The report returns tokens only. The code also returns the span of text each token covers, with the space before a word left out, which is what the morpheme metrics read.

Difference from predecessor

Against Character BPE: the symbols are bytes, and the space before a word is part of it.

Character BPE1 and 5:words are counted after normalising the text and splitting it into words and punctuation, and V starts from the characters seen
Byte-level BPE1 and 5:words keep the space before them and are written as their bytes, and V starts from the 256 byte symbols

Effect. Every character can be spelled, so there is no unknown token, and a piece knows whether it begins a word.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. Byte-level BPE training

Require: corpus D, vocabulary size B, special tokens S

Ensure: vocabulary V, ordered merges M

  1. f(w)← count of each word w in D, each word keeping the space before it and written as its byte symbols▷ hf_bpe.py:40
  2. for all words w do
  3. (c1)←(w)
  4. add f(w) to f(c1)
  5. V←S followed by the 256 byte symbols, M←()▷ hf_bpe.py:45
  6. n(a,b)←∑cf(c) times the places where a is followed by b inside c
  7. while |V|<B and some pair has a count do▷ hf_bpe.py:42-43
  8. (a*,b*)← the pair with the highest n, a tie going to the pair whose symbols entered V first
  9. join a*b* in every chunk that holds it, and update n
  10. append (a*,b*) to M, add the joined symbol to V
  11. return a standard BPE model holding S, V and M, with a byte-level decoder▷ hf_bpe.py:41-49

Reading Algorithm 1

1Words are counted once, so the rest works on distinct words with a weight. A space is put before every line, and the text is cut into words, numbers and runs of punctuation, each keeping the space before it. Every piece is then written as the printable form of its UTF-8 bytes. The text is not normalised, so a letter written in decomposed form keeps its bytes.2–4Every word is one chunk, as in Character BPE.5The special tokens take the first places and the 256 byte symbols follow, whether or not a byte occurs in the corpus. The order fixes how a tie is broken.6Pairs are counted inside chunks only. The space before a word is inside the chunk, so a merge may absorb it, and no merge ever spans two words.7–10Each round joins one pair everywhere and records it. The loop ends when the vocabulary is full or no pair is left.11The trained model is the vocabulary and the merges. The decoder turns the printable byte symbols back into text.

Algorithm 2. Byte-level BPE encoding

Require: text t, vocabulary V, ordered merges M

Ensure: the tokens of t, each with the span of t it covers

  1. put a space before t and split it into words, numbers and runs of punctuation, each keeping its space▷ hf_bpe.py:40
  2. write every piece as its byte symbols
  3. for all pieces p do
  4. s← the byte symbols of p
  5. while some adjacent pair of s is in M do
  6. join the adjacent pair that comes earliest in M
  7. return every s in order, each with the span of t it covers▷ _hf_base.py:54-55

Reading Algorithm 2

1–2The text is cut into pieces the same way as in training. No piece can hold a byte outside V, so there is no unknown token.3–6Merges are replayed in the order they were learned. These lines run inside the HuggingFace tokenizers library, so they cite no project code.7What is left when no learned pair remains is the token sequence. Each token also reports which characters of the text it covers, with the space before a word left out. That span is how the morpheme metrics find its cuts without reading the byte symbols.

Worked example

The corpus holds six forms of two nouns: hiša (house) five times, hiše four, hišo three, miza (table) four, mize three, mizo twice. The vocabulary size is 263: the 256 byte symbols, the unknown token the sweep reserves, and room for six merges. The tokenizer is the project's own backend, and the tables are written by the example script, which also checks that every merge is a most frequent pair. In the tables Ġ is the space before a word and Å¡ the two bytes of š.

The first four merges rebuild the stem hiš with its space: the two letters hi, the two bytes of š, the space onto hi, and the whole. Five of the six choices are ties, and each falls to the pair whose symbols entered the vocabulary first. At merge 1 the pair hi beats the pair of space and h, because the printable ASCII bytes enter the vocabulary before the space marker. Merges 5 and 6 rebuild miz, but no slot is left to join its space, so every form of miza starts with a lone space token.

The letter q never occurred in the corpus and is spelled as its own byte, not as an unknown token. The unseen word čas costs five tokens for three letters, because č is two bytes and neither pair was ever merged. The morpheme metrics see č as one piece, since both byte tokens report the same span. The form mize shows a cut after m that is not in the tokens. The lone space token reports the span of the first letter, and the metrics read a boundary from it.

Evidence

No experiment varies this entry yet.

Limits

A letter outside ASCII costs two symbols

š, č and ž are two bytes each, so a merge is spent on rebuilding every such letter before a stem that holds it can form. Until that merge is learned, a token can be half a character and cannot be read on its own.

The same word is spelled two ways

A word keeps the space before it, so hiša after a space and hiša right after an opening bracket or a quote are different symbol strings and may cut differently. Character BPE does not see the space and spells both alike.

A lone space token adds a false cut

When the space before a word was never merged into a piece, the token holding it reports the span of the word's first letter. The morpheme metrics then read a boundary after that letter, as mize shows in the worked example.

The vocabulary never falls below 256 symbols

All byte symbols are kept, including the many that only ever appear as the second byte of a letter. A small vocabulary spends a fixed share on symbols that never stand alone in Slovenian text.
