Kev

from paperin topic Typed Decision Modelsvariant of Jev
In one lineAn open Jev-like family on Qwen bases that packs the state and every question's option list into one causal sequence under a block mask, scores each option's closing token against the question's decide token with a pointer head, and is trained with cross-entropy through a low-rank adapter.
DescriptionDifferenceAlgorithmWorked exampleWhere it sitsEvidenceLimitsRelatedjk sections

Description

Kev is a family of decision models built by Jared Palmer on Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 bases, in four sizes from 0.8 to 27 billion parameters, that answer the same typed questions as Jev. The design follows the reconstruction of Jev's architecture: the state is written once at the front of the sequence, each question follows as its own branch holding the instructions and every option between marker tokens, and an attention mask lets a branch read the state and itself but never another branch. A small pointer head then compares the hidden state of each option's closing marker with the hidden state of a decide marker at the end of the branch, and a softmax over those comparisons is the question's distribution.

Three choices keep the recipe cheap and open to inspection.

  • The base stays frozen. Only a low-rank adapter of rank 16 on the attention, feed-forward and recurrent projections, and the pointer head, are trained. The 27 billion model is the exception and fine-tunes every weight.
  • Options are text, not slots. The head has no fixed output layer, so a question may bring any number of options and any wording. A yes-or-no question is two options, false and true; a score question lists its levels as options.
  • Training and serving share one text format. A training example is an API request with a label on every question, so the model never sees a layout at training time that it does not see when served.

Why it matters here

Kev is the cheapest documented way to turn an existing small decoder into a decision model: a short adapter run on one GPU, with the recipe, the data builders and the evaluation suites public. The option text is read in context, so nothing in the head is tied to English, and a Slovenian base or a Slovenian fine-tune would reuse the whole pipeline. The published per-stage data and learning rates give a starting point for a fine-tune on Slovenian labelled decisions.

Facts

Question typeschoice over named options; Noul as the two options false and true; score with each level an option, the answer being the expected level
BackboneQwen3.5 base at 0.8, 4 and 9 billion parameters, and the post-trained Qwen3.8 at 27 billion; a low-rank adapter of rank 16 and scale 32 on the attention, feed-forward and recurrent projections, with the base frozen except for the 27 billion model
Where an option is readthe hidden state of the option's closing marker token, scored against the hidden state of the question's decide token by a bilinear pointer head of width 256
Options per questionas many as fit the question's token budget of 8,192 tokens; the served protocol allows 255
Isolation between questionsexact; a block-causal mask on attention-only bases, and one row per question with the state's cache reused on bases with recurrent layers, with each question's positions restarting right after the state
Training objectivecross-entropy on the correct option, with the adapter and head trained together; optional Brier, ordinal and label-smoothing terms exist in the code and the released models do not use them
Calibrationone scalar temperature per checkpoint, fitted on held-out labelled rows and dividing the logits at inference; confidence as the vendor adapter's formula
Training dataa base set of 10,000 examples from ten public datasets, 896 generated policy examples and 1,680 examples from 60 generated rule structures, two epochs; then short follow-up stages from the released checkpoint on generated cases with day counts or removed evidence, 5,219 real consumer-finance complaints and generated tool-use data; no Jev outputs
Context lengthstates of up to 65,536 tokens served, plus 8,192 per question; the base stage trains on states of at most 384 tokens and the document stages on at most 7,552, and the 27 billion model on up to 32,768
WeightsApache-2.0 adapters and heads on Hugging Face under jaredpalmer, with the 27 billion model as full weights

Paper vs code
no paper. Against the README, the code also offers an option-isolation mode in which an option span sees only the state, the instructions and itself and all option spans share one position range, which makes the scores order-invariant; the released models do not use it. The README says training is plain cross-entropy; the loss function also accepts a soft target distribution, used for generated examples that carry one

Difference from predecessor

Against Jev: the score of an option is a match between two token states, not a row of a fixed output layer.

Jev8:zk←Whk+b, one score per answer read from the branch's final state
Kev8:zk,o←(Wkhk,o)⊤(Wqhk)/dp, the option's closing token matched against the decide token

Effect. Any number of options with any wording fits the head, and an option's score depends on its own text.

Algorithm

Algorithm 1. Kev: one pass over the state and every question, read by a pointer head

Require: state x; questions q1,…,qQ with instructions tk and options Ok; adapted decoder f; pointer head Wq,Wk of width dp; temperature T

Ensure: a distribution pk over Ok for every question

  1. S← \texttt{} and the tokens of x, cut to the state limit; segment 0, positions 0,…,|S|−1
  2. for all questions qk do
  3. Bk← \texttt{} tk, then \texttt{} o \texttt{} for each o∈Ok, then \texttt{}; segment k, positions restarting at |S|
  4. mask: token i may attend to token j≤i when j is in the state or in i's own segment
  5. H←f(SB1⋯BQ) under the mask; on a base with recurrent layers, each SBk runs as its own row with the state's cache reused
  6. for all questions qk do
  7. hk←H[k] and hk,o←H[k,o] for each option
  8. zk,o←(Wkhk,o)⊤(Wqhk)/dp
  9. pk←softmax(zk/T)
  10. return p1,…,pQ

    11. Reading Algorithm 1

    1The state opens the sequence behind one marker token. A state longer than the limit is cut, or refused when the caller asks for strictness.2** and **3Each question is appended as a branch. The branch's positions start where the state ended, so every question sits at the same distance from the state whatever came before it in the sequence.4The mask is causal within the state and within a branch, and a branch may read the state. A branch never reads another branch, which is what makes the questions independent of one another.5One forward pass gives every token a hidden state. The recurrent layers of the newer Qwen bases ignore attention masks, so there each question is its own row, state first, and the state's cache is computed once and reused. The two forms agree to rounding.6** to **8The pointer head projects the decide token as a query and every closing option marker as a key, and their scaled product is the option's score. The decide token comes last in its branch, so it has read every option before it is compared with each.9A softmax over the question's scores is its distribution. The temperature is one during training and a fitted constant when served, so the argmax never changes.10Every question's distribution is returned in one response. A score question's answer is the expected level under its distribution, and a yes-or-no question returns the probability of true.

    Algorithm 2. Kev training: cross-entropy through the adapter and the head

    Require: records of labelled questions; frozen base; adapter of rank 16; two epochs; held-out labelled rows

    Ensure: adapter, pointer head and temperature T

    1. for all batches of records do
    2. zk← the scores of Algorithm 1 with T=1 for every question k
    3. ℓ←∑k−logsoftmax(zk)[yk], or −∑odk,ologsoftmax(zk)[o] when a question carries a target distribution dk
    4. update the adapter and the head by AdamW on ℓ, clipping the gradient norm
    5. T←\argminT∑−logsoftmax(z/T)[y] over the held-out rows
    6. return adapter, head, T

    Reading Algorithm 2

    1** and **2Training runs the same packing and readout as serving, with the temperature at one so that the fitted value keeps its meaning.3The loss is the negative log probability of the labelled option. Generated examples may carry a whole target distribution instead of one label, and then the loss is the cross-entropy against it.4Only the adapter and the head move. The 27 billion model trains every weight at a much lower learning rate instead.5After training, one scalar temperature is fitted by likelihood on labelled rows the model did not train on. It changes how sure the model says it is and never which option it picks.6The checkpoint is the adapter, the head and the temperature; the base is downloaded separately.

    Worked example

    The example script ports the packing rule to a record whose tokens are words: a three-word state and two questions, one with two named options and one yes-or-no question.

    Both questions' positions restart at four, right after the state, so each question is laid out as if it were the only one. The decide token of the second question sees the four state tokens and its own ten tokens, and none of the first question's. The pointer head compares it with the two closing option markers of its own question only.

    Where it sits

    Kev serves the same endpoint as Jev, so the official TypeSafe client runs against it unchanged. Inside, it is a stock Qwen decoder with an adapter and a head of a few million parameters, so any tooling that serves Qwen serves Kev. The repository ships a fine-tuning path that starts from a released checkpoint, fits the temperature on a held-out slice of the user's own labels, and scores the result against the untouched model.

    Evidence

    No experiment varies this entry yet.

    Limits

    Options still see one another

    Isolation is exact between questions and absent within one. The decide token attends to the whole option list, so reordering options can change their scores, and the released models do not use the order-invariant mode.

    The temperature is fitted elsewhere

    One scalar temperature fitted on the author's held-out suites does not transfer to a deployer's workload, and the repository documents a case where the served confidence sits well above the accuracy on a new dataset. The repository therefore ships a per-workload refit.

    English and short states

    The released models are trained on English and on states of at most a few thousand tokens. Longer states are served, but the model cards validate accuracy only up to 8,192 tokens for the three smaller sizes.

    Day arithmetic and removed evidence

    The models answer poorly when a decision needs the number of days between two dates, which a preprocessor can add, and when the deciding evidence is absent from the state, which the follow-up stages train against but do not remove.

    Von

    from paperin topic Typed Decision ModelsarXiv:2609.30243
    In one lineAn open decision model on a ModernBERT-large encoder that packs question, state and options into one sequence with a mask token before each option, scores each mask token's state with a small head while each option attends only to the state and itself, trains with cross-entropy plus a Brier term, and reports confidence through a temperature that depends on the request.
    DescriptionAlgorithmWorked exampleWhere it sitsEvidenceLimitsjk sections

    Description

    Von answers the same typed questions as Jev with a bidirectional encoder of 395 million parameters instead of a decoder. The question's instructions and the state form a prefix. After a separator, every option is written out behind a mask token, the token a masked language model was trained to fill. One encoder pass gives each mask token a hidden state that has read the prefix and its own option, and a two-layer head turns that state into one score. A softmax over the scores is the question's distribution.

    Three choices distinguish it from a decoder with a pointer head.

    • Options cannot see one another. From version 1.2 the attention mask lets an option token attend to the prefix and to its own option span only, and every option span restarts at the same position. An option's score is therefore a function of the prefix and that option alone, and reordering the options cannot change any score.
    • Digits are single tokens. Every run of digits is split into single characters before tokenisation, because the encoder's vocabulary cuts numbers inconsistently and the model could not learn arithmetic over them.
    • Confidence tracks the request. The softmax temperature is not a constant but a bounded linear function of the answer's entropy, the length of the state and the number of options, fitted on labelled items.

    A yes-or-no question is two described options. When the caller gives no descriptions, the model also scores the same question against an empty state and subtracts part of that context-free preference, because the model prefers yes with no state at all.

    Why it matters here

    Von is the open model in this topic whose backbone is closest to what this project trains: a masked-language encoder of the ModernBERT generation. Its head and packing need nothing from the encoder beyond a mask token and hidden states, so the same design would sit on a Slovenian encoder. The repository's fine-tuning guide names a fresh head on another encoder for another language as a supported route, with the English corpus as the base and the language's own labelled rows added on top.

    Facts

    Question typeschoice over described options; Noul as two described options, true first, with a context-free bias subtracted when no descriptions are given; score over levels, returning the expected level
    BackboneModernBERT-large, 395 million parameters, every weight fine-tuned; a multilingual sibling, Laya, uses mmBERT-base, and the repository's guide trains a fresh head on other masked-language encoders
    Where an option is readthe hidden state of the mask token placed before the option's text, through a normalised two-layer head to one logit
    Options per questionbounded by the 8,192-token sequence; the authors recommend few
    Isolation between questionscomplete, one encoder pass per question; within a question an option attends only to the prefix and itself, with its positions reset, so the scores are order-invariant
    Training objectivecross-entropy plus half the Brier score against the target distribution over the options, accepting a soft target
    Calibrationtemperature T=θ0+θ1H^+θ2log10(state tokens)/4+θ3K/8, with H^ the normalised entropy of the raw distribution and K the option count, clamped to [0.3,12] and fitted by likelihood on labelled items; confidence as the vendor adapter's formula; a yes-or-no probability is pushed out of a band around one half before it is returned
    Training dataabout 290,000 balanced decision items across operational, security, moderation, semantic, triage and adversarial families, the semantic part including the ANLI and WANLI entailment sets as yes-or-no questions; 40,000 long-context items and 40,000 synthetic two-hop and numeric items; no item of the JevBench benchmark
    Context length8,192 tokens; a longer state is cut in the middle
    WeightsApache-2.0 on Hugging Face as wfzyx/von, about three gigabytes

    Paper vs code
    no paper. Against the model card, the code computes the confidence with the option-count formula of the vendor adapter and not a top-two margin; the card does not mention the empty-state pass that debiases a yes-or-no question without descriptions, nor the band that moves a returned yes-or-no probability away from one half, both of which the code applies by default

    Algorithm

    Algorithm 1. Von: option-marker scoring in one encoder pass

    Require: state x; question t; options o1,…,oK with descriptions; encoder E; head g; temperature map θ

    Ensure: a distribution p over the options and a confidence c

    1. s←t x \texttt{[SEP]} \texttt{[MASK]} o1 \texttt{[MASK]} o2⋯ \texttt{[MASK]} oK, with every digit its own token and any marker string inside user text broken
    2. mask: a prefix token attends to the prefix; an option token attends to the prefix and to its own span
    3. positions: every option span restarts at the prefix length; the local-attention window is measured on these positions
    4. H←E(s) under the mask and positions
    5. zk←g(H[[MASK]k]) for k=1,…,K
    6. T←clamp(θ0+θ1H^(z)+θ2log10|x|/4+θ3K/8, 0.3, 12)
    7. p←softmax(z/T) and c←(Kmaxp−1)/(K−1)
    8. return \argmaxz, p, c; for a score question also ∑k(k−1)pk

    Reading Algorithm 1

    1The whole question is one string. The prefix is instructions then state, and each option follows a mask token. Digits are split so that the same number tokenises the same way wherever it appears. A literal mask or separator string in user text is broken, so a document cannot add a phantom option.2** and **3The mask and the positions together make each option's computation independent of the other options. Blocking attention alone is not enough, because rotary positions encode distance and an option's distance from the prefix would still depend on how many option tokens sit before it.4** and **5One pass gives every token a state. The head reads the mask token in front of each option, the position a masked language model learned to fill from context, and returns one score per option.6The temperature is computed from the request itself. A flat raw distribution, a long state and many options each raise it, so the model claims less than its raw scores suggest where it tends to be wrong.7The scaled scores become probabilities and the confidence is the top probability rescaled by the option count. The temperature is monotone, so the chosen option is the argmax of the raw scores either way.8The chosen option, the distribution and the confidence are returned. A score question's answer is the expected level.

    Algorithm 2. Von training: cross-entropy plus Brier over the option markers

    Require: labelled items (x,t,O,y), some with a target distribution d; encoder and head initialised from the previous release; Brier weight 0.5

    Ensure: fine-tuned encoder and head, then a fitted map θ

    1. for all batches do
    2. z← lines 1 to 5 of Algorithm 1; p←softmax(z); d← one-hot y unless the item carries a target distribution
    3. ℓ←mean(−∑kdklogpk)+0.5mean(∑k(pk−dk)2)
    4. update every weight of the encoder and the head
    5. θ←\argminθ∑−logsoftmax(z/Tθ)[y] over labelled items, with the weights frozen
    6. return encoder, head, θ

    Reading Algorithm 2

    1** and **2Training packs and scores exactly as serving does, at a temperature of one. The target is the labelled option, or a whole distribution when the item was built with one.3The loss adds a Brier term, the squared distance between the predicted and the target distribution, to the cross-entropy. The Brier score is a proper scoring rule, which rewards reporting the frequency one actually observes, and it penalises a confident wrong answer more than the cross-entropy alone does near certainty.4The encoder is not frozen. The released weights are a full retrain from the previous release with the independent-options mask on.5The temperature map is fitted afterwards on labelled items, by the likelihood of the correct option, with a scalar temperature fitted beside it and the better one under cross-validation kept.6The checkpoint holds the encoder, the head and the map, and the map can be refitted on a deployer's labels without touching the weights.

    Worked example

    The example script runs the released calibration module with the map shipped in the Von 1.2 checkpoint on one set of raw scores for three options, with the state at three lengths.

    The raw scores do not change, so the chosen option does not change. The temperature rises with the length of the state, from about three at forty tokens to about nine at four thousand, and the reported confidence falls from 0.21 to 0.08. The model says less about a long state because, on the items the map was fitted on, it was right less often there.

    Where it sits

    Von serves the same endpoint as Jev and ships as a Python and TypeScript package. Inside, it is a stock ModernBERT encoder with a head of a few hundred thousand parameters, run once per question on CPU or GPU. A tiered confidence gate in the package splits answers into those taken automatically and those escalated, at a cutoff the repository measured on held-out items.

    Evidence

    No experiment varies this entry yet.

    Limits

    English only

    The encoder and the corpus are English. Other languages get token matching with a confidence the map never saw, and the multilingual sibling Laya on mmBERT-base is a separate model with its own weights.

    The map is fitted on one distribution

    The temperature map is fitted on benchmark items. The repository's own threshold sweep finds that on out-of-domain probes the ranking by confidence breaks and no cutoff keeps accuracy, so a deployer refits the map on labels.

    A yes-or-no question without descriptions is weak

    With no descriptions, the two options are generic and surface cues win. The empty-state debiasing and the band around one half are repairs on top of that, and the band means the returned probability is no longer the calibrated one.

    An option is judged alone

    Blocking cross-option attention buys order invariance and loses the ability to judge an option relative to the others. A question whose answer is "the better of these two" is read as two separate judgements.

    experiments/GLOSSARY.md

    Glossary

    Metrics 35Terms 86

    Metrics

    Precision
    Of the items the system returned, the share that are correct. 1 means nothing wrong was returned.
    used in KPI coverage check, Curation quality, Curation thresholds, Sloleks morph gold, BPE-knockout, Morfessor pre-tokenization
    Recall
    Of the correct items, the share the system returned. 1 means nothing was missed.
    used in KPI coverage check, GLiNER2.5, BPE-knockout, Morfessor pre-tokenization
    F1 F1 score
    Harmonic mean of precision and recall; 1 is perfect, 0 means nothing right. Macro F1 averages F1 over classes or units with equal weight; micro F1 pools all decisions first.
    used in Slovene tokenizer choice, KPI coverage check, Sloleks morph gold, BPE-knockout, MorphBPE
    Macro-F1
    The F1 score computed per class and averaged with equal weight per class, so a rare class such as medical counts as much as a frequent one.
    used in KPI coverage check
    Precision@k P@k
    Precision over the top k ranked items only.
    Recall@k R@k
    The share of correct items found within the top k.
    Accuracy
    The share of all decisions that are correct; misleading when classes are imbalanced.
    used in Open Slovene data survey, DeBERTa V2, DeBERTa, Type-safe encoder models, BPE-knockout, CLM, Kev, Von
    Cohen's κ κ, kappa
    Agreement between two raters beyond what chance would give; 1 is full agreement, 0 chance level, below 0 worse than chance.
    used in Curation quality, Curation thresholds
    Quadratic-weighted κ weighted kappa
    Cohen's κ for an ordered scale such as 1-5, where a disagreement costs the square of its distance, so a one-point miss counts far less than a three-point one.
    Wilson interval Wilson score interval
    A confidence interval for a share that, unlike the textbook one, never runs below 0 or above 1, which matters for shares near either end.
    used in Curation quality, Curation thresholds
    Drop precision
    Of the documents a curation stage dropped, the share judged bad text; high means the stage removes what it should.
    used in Curation quality
    Target precision
    Of the documents a content filter dropped, the share judged to carry what that filter is built to catch — not Slovene for the language filter, spam for the spam filter, ill-formed text for the quality filter, repeated furniture for the repetition filter.
    Residual bad rate
    Of the documents a curation stage kept, the share judged bad text; what the stage failed to catch.
    Kept win rate
    Of the pairs of one kept and one dropped document from the same source and stage, the share where the judge prefers the kept one in both presentation orders.
    Order disagreement
    The share of pairs whose answer changes when the two documents swap places; it measures the judge's position bias.
    Side-with-judge share
    Of the cases where the judge and the pipeline conflict, the share where a person labelling blind agrees with the judge.
    Twin match rate
    Of a dedup stage's dropped documents, the share whose content survives in the finished corpus as another copy — byte-identical for exact dedup, sharing at least half its three-sentence windows for sentence dedup.
    Window coverage
    The share of a document's three-sentence windows that another document also contains.
    Retention
    The share of a source's converted documents that reach the finished corpus.
    used in Curation thresholds
    Type-token ratio TTR
    Distinct tokens divided by tokens; it falls as a sample grows, so it is only compared at one fixed token budget.
    Out-of-vocabulary rate OOV rate
    The share of alphabetic tokens a lexicon does not list; names, foreign words, code and encoding damage all count as out of vocabulary.
    CPU hours
    Processor time a step consumed, summed over its tasks; comparable between steps and machines.
    used in KPI coverage check, Curation quality
    Wall hours wall clock
    Elapsed time a step took on the machine that ran it, at the worker count it was given.
    Agresti–Coull interval Agresti–Coull adjustment
    A normal-approximation confidence interval for a share that first adds about two successes and two failures, so a share of 0 or 1 still gets a width; summed over independent shares, it gives the interval on a total such as bad text gained.
    Share needed
    The target divided by the count, the lowest share of a count that must truly belong to its domain for the count to stay above the target; a share above 1 means the count falls short even if every item is right.
    Kendall's τ Kendall, Kendall tau, rank agreement
    Agreement between two rankings of the same items, the share of item pairs ordered alike minus the share ordered oppositely; 1 is the same order, 0 unrelated, −1 reversed.
    used in Sloleks morph gold
    Bootstrap bootstrap interval
    A confidence interval found by redrawing the scored items with replacement many times and recomputing the statistic on each draw; the interval spans the middle 95% of those values.
    used in Slovene tokenizer choice, Sloleks morph gold
    Morpheme-boundary F1 morph boundary F1, MorphScore
    F1 of the cuts a tokenizer makes inside a word against the cuts a morphological gold makes there, pooled over all scored forms.
    used in Sloleks morph gold, BPE-knockout
    Morph-Edit-Distance
    The number of token insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn a word's tokens into its gold morphemes, averaged over forms; lower is closer to the gold.
    used in Slovene tokenizer choice, Sloleks morph gold
    Morph-Consistency
    F1 of whether two words that share a gold morpheme also share a token, over sampled word pairs; high means a morpheme is spelled by the same token wherever it appears. Pairs are drawn per shared morpheme, at most 200 each, so on a stem-ending gold the many stems outweigh the few endings.
    used in Sloleks morph gold
    Fertility
    Tokens per word over a held-out text sample; 1 means every word is one token, and higher means words are cut into more pieces.
    used in Sloleks morph gold
    Compression characters per token, bytes per token, tokens per byte
    How much text one token covers on a held-out sample; higher means shorter token sequences.
    used in Slovene tokenizer choice, Sloleks morph gold
    Rényi efficiency
    Rényi entropy of the token frequencies (order 2.5) divided by its maximum for the vocabulary size; it is high when tokens are used evenly, low when a few tokens dominate.
    used in Sloleks morph gold, Morfessor pre-tokenization
    Quarter rule levelled off, still improving, no early gain
    The levelling rule of the vocabulary sweep. A metric has levelled off for an algorithm when its gain from 64k to 128k is under a quarter of its gain from 16k to 32k; it falls when that late gain is negative, and the rule does not apply when there was no early gain.
    used in Slovene tokenizer choice, Sloleks morph gold
    Off-source precision precision off the source, off-source read
    A domain's precision read only on documents whose source carries a different label, so the classifier has to find the domain from the text rather than inherit it from the source.
    used in KPI coverage check

    Terms

    CJVT
    The Centre for Language Resources and Technologies of the University of Ljubljana, which maintains Sloleks.
    used in Open Slovene data survey, Sloleks morph gold
    q05, q50, q95 q05, q50, q95
    The 5th, 50th (median) and 95th percentiles of a distribution.
    Curation pipeline
    The eight stages that turn extracted text into the pretraining corpus, in order convert, language, spam, quality, repetition, exact dedup, sentence dedup and statistics; the six from language to sentence dedup each keep or drop every document.
    Content filter
    One of the four curation stages that judge a document's content — the language, spam, quality and repetition filters — as opposed to the two dedup stages, which remove copies.
    Gopher heuristics Gopher-style, quality filter, repetition filter
    The rule-based quality and repetition filters published with DeepMind's Gopher model — thresholds on document length, word length, symbol ratios and repeated n-grams, tuned on English web text.
    used in Slovene training data, KPI coverage check, Curation quality, Curation thresholds
    Letter rule letter share
    The Gopher quality rule that most words contain a letter, meant to catch tables of numbers and symbol junk; the letter share is the share of a document's words that contain a letter, and the rule drops the document when it falls under 0.8.
    used in Curation thresholds
    Route curation route, raw-crawl route, curated-prose route, medical-and-academic route
    A named set of content-filter settings that every source of one kind shares in the curation pipeline, so a web crawl and an edited corpus are filtered differently. Not the repository's conversion routes, which are the three output trees that fork after extraction.
    used in Slovene training data, Curation thresholds, CLM, Jev, Von
    Raw web crawl web crawl, web crawls
    A source scraped from the open web with little editing — here c4, cc100, culturax, fineweb2, hplt, macocu_sl, classla_web_sl and finepdf. In the curation-thresholds experiment finepdf, a crawl of PDF documents, takes the curated-prose route.
    used in Slovene training data, Open Slovene data survey, KPI coverage check, Curation quality, Curation thresholds, Sloleks morph gold
    Curated source
    A source assembled or edited by people for a purpose — here the parliamentary, medical, legal, scientific, news, wiki and reference corpora. In the curation-thresholds experiment the medical and academic ones take a route of their own.
    Sloleks
    The reference lexicon of Slovene word forms, used here to check whether a token is an ordinary Slovene word.
    used in Slovene tokenizer choice, Open Slovene data survey, Curation quality, Sloleks morph gold, Morfessor pre-tokenization, MorphBPE, MorphPiece
    LLM judge judge
    A language model given a fixed rubric and asked to label documents, standing in for a human annotator once its agreement with one is measured.
    used in Slovene training data, KPI coverage check, Curation quality, Curation thresholds, Von
    Bad text lenient bar, strict bar
    At the lenient bar, a document the judge scores coherence 2 or lower, labels garbage or boilerplate, or flags as adult or spam; the strict bar also counts coherence 3.
    used in Curation quality, Curation thresholds
    Coherence
    The rubric's 1-5 score of whether a document reads as connected, sensible text, from unreadable (1) to fluent, well-formed prose (5).
    used in Curation quality, Curation thresholds
    Boilerplate
    Text furniture rather than written content — menus, footers, cookie notices, navigation, templated disclaimers.
    used in Slovene training data, KPI coverage check, Curation quality, Curation thresholds
    Calibration set
    Documents labelled by both a person and the judge, so their agreement is known before the judge's labels are used as evidence.
    used in Curation quality
    Adjudication set
    Documents drawn where the judge and the pipeline flatly disagree, labelled by a person to settle which of the two is right.
    Stratified sample
    A fixed number of documents from every source, stage and decision, so small sources are represented; its rates describe each cell, not the corpus as a whole.
    Pairwise comparison
    The judge is shown two documents and asked which is better, or whether they tie; each pair is asked twice with the documents swapped.
    Position bias
    A judge's tendency to prefer whichever document it is shown first (or second), regardless of content.
    used in Curation quality
    Grill grill round
    A structured design interview that questions a plan one decision at a time; a history line's Q15 names its fifteenth question.
    used in Curation quality
    SLING
    The Slovenian national supercomputing network, whose clusters the project can use for jobs that do not fit on one machine.
    used in Slovene training data, Curation quality
    Gated source
    A dataset whose licence restricts redistribution, so it is counted separately from what a public release could hold.
    KPI KPI 2, KPI 3, KPI 4
    A key performance indicator the ARIS proposal (Z2-70067) commits the project to. KPI 2 asks for more than 10,000 examples in each of at least two domains, medicine and science; KPI 3 for more than 5B tokens per language; KPI 4 for more than 500,000 tokens per domain.
    used in Slovene training data, Open Slovene data survey, KPI coverage check, Curation thresholds
    Access filter open, open+login, all
    Which datasets a total counts. open is what anyone can download, open+login adds what a registered user can, all adds gated and not-downloadable sources — what exists rather than what is reachable.

    The baseline build is the shared corpus rebuilt at the pipeline's settings on main, with no per-source routes; the frozen build is the candidate corpus built with the route settings frozen before the fresh draw; the loosened build relaxes its quality and repetition settings per route and is built into its own folder beside it.

    A shortfall against a target in a domain that never had the material before curation, so only new sources can close it.
